paragraphs.text: We must speak about the varied plague of heresies and the different errors that arose from the beginning of the world, that flowed on under the Jews, and that have sprung up since our Lord Jesus the Saviour came in the flesh. We must set out their number step by step, and recognize that the holy prophet was right to compare the enemy of the human race [the devil] to a partridge.

For the [partridge], since it is often barren, [?] secretly broods over the young of other birds. For a time it cherishes them and claims them as its own offspring. But once they have grown old enough to tell the difference, they abandon their false parents. Remembering by their own instinct the claims of their true parents, and seeing them plainly with their own eyes, they no longer hesitate to follow them. For whose sake was this comparison given to us?

It was because, once the devil had been left behind, on account of the impiety of the one who thought he held the whole world under his sway and power, [?] but afterwards, when Christ the parent had been seen and recognized by us, every human being casts off the falsehood of that most lying parent, recognizes the true parent, Christ, and no longer delays to follow in his footsteps. For we see every day how the prophecy of the most blessed Jeremiah is fulfilled in a figure, which says: "The partridge cried out; it gathered what it did not bring forth, getting riches for itself without wisdom. In the middle of its days they will leave it, and at its end it will be a fool."

For now all the nations are daily abandoning the deadly idolatry of the enemy. From the law and the prophets they hear that Christ is true God, and they believe and remember that he is always with the Father. So they all hasten in every way to fly to him as suppliants, that the prophecy may be fulfilled: "All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord Christ."
THIS, THEN, IS THE LIST OF HERETICS FROM THE BEGINNING AND ORIGIN OF THE WORLD:

FIRST are the Ophites, who are also called Serpentines. They venerate the serpent, that is, the snake, saying that it was the first to bring us the beginning of the knowledge of good and evil. They therefore assert that God envied it, because, they say, it was the first to bring the woman the knowledge of good and evil, and through her that knowledge spread to the whole human race.

That, they say, is why it was cast down from the first heaven into another. So they claim that it will also come from heaven. They consider it to be some power of God, and they proclaim that it should be worshipped.
Others are the Cainites, who praise Cain the fratricide, the firstborn of our father, the blessed Adam, the first-formed man. They say that Cain was made by one
power, namely the devil's, while the most blessed Abel was born of another. They say that the greater power, the one that was in Cain, prevailed, so that he killed his brother.

Another heresy is that of the Sethians. They venerate by name Seth, the son of Adam who was born later and given this name, born after the killing of the most blessed Abel. From him they are called Sethians, because they worship him. They say that when two men had been created at the beginning, and the angels had fallen into dissension, a female power prevailed in heaven. For among them males and females are thought to be gods and goddesses.

Seeing this, they say, and seeing that Abel the just had been killed, the Mother planned to bring forth the just Seth, and placed in him the spirit of a great power, so that, they say, the hostile powers might be destroyed.
They say that Christ, who is God, traces his descent from this same Seth. Some of them, however, assert and hold not only that Christ descends from him, but that Seth is Christ himself.
Afterwards a certain Dositheus, a Jew by race, dared to say that one should live only according to the flesh. He did not hope for a future resurrection in the law of God or on its basis,
he did not believe in the Spirit of God or in angels, and he did not expect the future judgment taught in the law and the prophets.

After him came the Sadducees, named after Zadok, a Jew who bore that name. He was Dositheus' disciple and he established this heresy, so that from him they were called Sadducees. They likewise preach that one should live only according to the flesh, be circumcised, and have one's body washed,

and they expect nothing else from the divine law, following the madness of Epicurus rather than the ordinances of the divine law. Of them it is also written in the gospel, where the Lord teaches and preaches against this pestilent heresy.
Another heresy is that of the Pharisees. It confesses a future resurrection and accepts the law and the prophets, but they expect the Christ as a righteous man.
They follow Jewish practice and do not accept the gospels, and they assert that certain times are opposed to Christ our Lord.

Others are the Samaritans, so named after King Samareus. Others say they were called Samaritans after a son of Canaan who bore the name Samareus. They accept the law of Moses, that is, only four books. They do not expect a future judgment, they deny the resurrection, and they do not believe in the Christ, God and Son of God, who was proclaimed beforehand in the law and the prophets.

Nor, according to the law, do they hold that a human being has an immortal soul. They think that one is to live only in this body, and they consider the future resurrection to be the begetting of children, which happens daily in this world. This is the folly they preach, and so they are like senseless beasts, as it is written in the prophet: "Man, set in honour, did not understand; he is compared to senseless beasts, and has become like them."
Another heresy of the Jews is that of those called Nazoraeans. It accepts the law and the prophets, but holds that one should live according to the flesh, and imagines that all justification con-

sists in fleshly observance. They also let the hair of their heads grow, thinking that the whole power of righteousness lies in this. They claim this token for themselves from Samson the judge, as if on the ground that he was called a Nazirite. Later the pagans borrowed from his figure and called strong men "Hercules."
Others again are those called Essenes. They live the life of monks. They do not eat delicate foods, take no pains over their clothing, and own nothing. They devote themselves to read-

ing and to good works, and live in secluded places. But they do not expect the Christ, God and Son of God, nor do they recognize him as the Lord proclaimed in the law and the prophets. Instead they believe in him and expect him only as a prophet or a righteous man.

Others are the Heliognostics, who are also called Deinvictiaci. They worship the sun, saying that the sun knows all the things of God, that nothing but the sun enlightens human beings, and that the sun provides them with all their nourishment. They do not recognize that the sun is a servant, running its course each day as appointed by God the Father through Christ the Lord in the Holy Spirit. Of him it is written: "He who commands the sun to rise, and it rises, and not to rise, and it does not rise."

It was the vain pagan Hermes Trismegistus who taught that, after almighty God, both he and all people should worship none other than the sun. When he went to the province of the Celts, he is known to have taught them and persuaded them to give in to this error. The captive Jews worshipped this sun, as the prophet Ezekiel condemns in his charge against those same Jews, declaring them guilty of treason against the divine majesty and solemnly convicting them, as it is written.
Others worship frogs, which at that time, under Pharaoh, the wrath of God poured over the land of the Egyptians, so that they might wear the Egyptians
out with their stench. They persist in this wickedness even now, thinking they can appease God's wrath by this empty observance.

Others are called Musiritae, who worship mice. Long ago, under Eli the priest, the ark of the covenant was captured by the Philistines, and through God's wrath the earth brought forth mice to destroy their crops. Warned by their own people, the Philistines made golden mice and sent them back, five of them, together with the ark and golden seats, and the plague left them.
These people, though they accept the law and the prophets, do not recognize that this is empty and abominable, something despised by everyone and ridiculed in every way.

Others worship the fly of Ekron, in the city of that name. As it is written in the book of Kings, Ozias, king of the Jews, being sick, sent to the fly of the city of Ekron to ask whether he could be healed of his bodily illness.

For this reason the blessed prophet Elijah, angered with divine zeal because the king of the Jews chose to hope for healing not from God, Christ, but from a fly and the city of Ekron, at once declared by the divine Spirit that the king would not escape, but would die in his bed.

There are the Troglodytes, as they are called among the Jews. Living in hidden caves, they did not cease to worship idols, as the prophet Ezekiel says, when the Lord showed him how the elders of the people, holding censers in hidden caves, offered sacrifice to idols and worshipped them with blinded minds.

There is another heresy among the Jews which [venerates] the Queen, whom they also call the Fortune of Heaven [?], and whom in Africa they call Caelestis. They do not hesitate to offer sacrifices to her. So it was that the Jews of that time spoke openly to the prophet Jeremiah, when he warned them to turn away from idols, serve the Lord, and worship him alone:

they cried out in anger, saying that ever since they stopped sacrificing to the Fortune or Queen of Heaven, every evil and danger had befallen them. For this reason the blessed Jeremiah went out from the people and from their city and wrote the Lamentations in a book on account of their impiety, and he announced that ruin would come upon them and their city before long.

Others among them, keeping alive the memory of Baal, the name of a king of Tyre, worshipped his idol and sacrificed to him, as is recorded in the book of Kings, when Ahab, king of the Israelites, and his wife Jezebel did not cease to sacrifice to that idol. Then the blessed prophet Elijah, moved by divine zeal and sent by Christ the Lord, spoke to those who confessed the law under the name of Judaism but served deadly pagan impiety. He said to all the people:

"Why do you limp on both your knees? Either God is God, or Baal is Baal." Nevertheless the king and queen kept favouring the priests of the groves, and they perished by various punishments and torments. The people, too, did not turn away from idols and perished in repeated captivities.

Others venerated Asthar, a man, and Camoth, the abomination of the Canaanites and Sidonians, that is, idols of men and women, and offered various sacrifices to them. Because of them, at that time, captivity often came upon those kings and the people by the Lord's permission, as is recorded in the books of Kings.

Except for the blessed King David, holy Hezekiah, Josiah, and Jehu son of Nimshi, all the others allowed the people to sacrifice to idols, and they too were often caught up [?] in the destruction of the people. They did not destroy the idols, but rather hurried to become patrons of the people's impiety, as the other kings did, as the books of Kings bear witness.

There is another heresy among the Jews, for which the Lord rebuked them through the prophets. The blessed martyr Stephen also reproached them for it, saying: "Did you offer me slain victims and sacrifices for forty years, O house of Israel, says the Lord almighty? And now you have taken up the tent of Moloch and the star of the god Remphan, the shapes of fixed idols and carved images?" Therefore the Lord says:
"I will make you captives by deportation into the land of Babylonia and of the Persians, and into other inland and dry places, to the farthest bounds of all the earth."

Others set up an altar called Topheth, after someone's name, in the valley of the son of Hinnom, and there [the Jews] sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons. Of them the Lord says through the prophet Ezekiel:

"Behold, son of man, see what the people of Israel are doing: they sacrifice their sons and daughters to demons in the valley of Topheth, though I did not command them to commit this iniquity among the people of Israel."

Others are the Puteorites, who worship wells. They dig them deep and draw from them as if it were the water of salvation, placing some hope in it, although the Lord says through the prophet in warning: "They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold the water of salvation."

What he had said beforehand through the prophet, he fulfilled when he was divinely present, saying: "Everyone who drinks of this earthly water will thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst, but it will become in him a spring welling up to eternal life." This was, of course, the Christian grace of saving baptism, granted to the human race by the Lord, the Saviour.

There is another heresy among the Jews which sacrificed to a serpent and practised this impiety of the serpent until the time of Hezekiah, the most blessed king of the Jews. As we read in the books of Kings, until Hezekiah the Jewish people sacrificed to the bronze serpent which the blessed Moses had been commanded to make when Israel came out of Egypt, when the Jews were grumbling and were being bitten by serpents and dying.

So the Lord commanded Moses to make a bronze serpent and hang it on a pole in the middle of the people, and those who looked at it were saved from the plagues and from their various wounds. To this bronze serpent the Jewish people sacrificed until King Hezekiah. The Jews also carved figures on a great stone like an obelisk, which stood in the temple as a pillar. On it they cut incisions and impressions by hand, like certain letters. They took various little figures from it, put them on a metal plate, and carried them around their necks.

They also taught incantations and kept these things as phylacteries, or rather used them as tools of sorcery, and devoutly honoured them. From this they carried, and still carry, amulets and charms on their bodies, which the Lord had everywhere forbidden in the law, because this was the impiety of pagan blindness.

The most blessed King Hezekiah therefore ordered these impressions or carvings to be erased, scraped off completely with iron, and cut away. He also commanded the bronze serpent to be taken down and broken. For this he was rightly delivered by the Lord from the great siege of the Persians and Assyrians, who had come at that time to take the Jewish people and their city captive. In that night, when King Hezekiah

feared the barbarians, an angel of the Lord came down from heaven and in the silence of the night struck down one hundred and eighty-five thousand foreigners who were besieging the city. In the morning he showed the king and the whole Jewish people all these men lifeless and dead.
There is another heresy, which the prophet Ezekiel saw at God's command: seventy elders of the Jews standing in a cave under the earth,
holding censers, sacrificing to various carved images and worshipping them.
There is another heresy of the Jews, which the prophet was made to see in a cave at God's command: women sitting and lamenting a certain Tammuz, who was the son of a king of the gentiles.

The Jewish women worshipped his image with weeping, practising the impiety of the gentiles, and did not cease to offer sacrifices to him. Tammuz was also the name of that Pharaoh, king of the Egyptians, who ruled over the Egyptians at that time, in the days of the blessed Moses.

There is another heresy among the Jews, who worshipped the idols of the Baalites as idols of many men and many women, and did not cease to offer sacrifices to them in hidden caves. Scripture speaks as if they were many, male and female.

This [?] or from King Belus, who for a long time held the East under his powerful rule. It showed that all their descendants came from his wife and from the sons and daughters born of these parents, so that from them they were called by the plural name Baalites.

For just as there is the family of the Greeks, or of the Anicii, and others, so all their descendants arose from their own parents, and from one name this impious race came to be called Baalites. So when they died and were placed in tombs, their descendants, buried likewise in that place, came to be called by this name by their people and by later generations, so that they were called Baalites after their original family.

Belus came to have this name or surname either as his own name or from his strength in war, because at that time he overcame many. The Jewish people are accused in divine Scripture of following the impiety of the gentiles in this matter, and because they sacrificed to these, that is, to the kings, their sons, and all their kindred after them, they were handed over to various captivities.

There is another heresy among the Jews which [worships] the idol Baal [?]. They claim it took its name from Balaam the false prophet, who came from Mesopotamia against the most blessed Moses, because Balak, king of the Moabites at that time, had asked him to come to him and curse the Jewish people.

In the Scriptures he was earlier called a prophet. But after he scorned the Lord's command, he sank to the ruin of a false prophet by plotting against God's people. So the Jews, making an idol of him under this name as the pagans do, did not cease to worship it.

There is another heresy [?] concerning the Pythoness: they covered a woman with garments and hoped to obtain certain answers from her. This is why they say that the Pythoness raised the soul of the blessed Samuel from the underworld, and very many people still suppose to this day that this can be believed above all. Their reason is that what the most blessed prophet had told King Saul while he was alive, he is known to have spoken again as true answers, as if from God, when he was raised.

Since very many prefer to accept this lie, they go down to everlasting ruin, though the prophet says: "The souls of the righteous are in the hand of the Lord, and death does not touch them." How then could an impious soul raise from the underworld a pious and holy soul, and above all a prophet's? But they do not know that souls which turn away from faith in Christ the Lord make themselves devoted to impiety and submit to it with all their zeal. For every human being has free will to choose what he wishes to do, with God's permission. [?] because he had turned away from the Lord, so that an unclean spirit now ruled over him, according to what the blessed Elijah said to those who wavered and limped in the divine law: "Either God is God, or Baal is Baal."

For whoever cleaves to Christ is one body with him, and whoever cleaves to an unclean spirit is of one mind with it. And when Ahab, king of the Jews, believed Zedekiah and other false prophets and despised Micaiah, the true prophet of the Lord, the Lord questioned an unclean spirit. Christ the Lord was still granting the king room for kindness for a time, so that if he chose to believe the true prophet he would escape the storm of danger, but if he refused and believed the false prophets instead, he would certainly perish.

So the Lord questions the unclean spirit, saying: "Who will deceive Ahab, king of the Israelites, so that he goes into battle and is killed there?" And behold, an unclean spirit came forward, saying: "I will go and do it." And the Lord said to the unclean spirit: "How will you do it?" And the unclean spirit said to the Lord: "I will make myself like an angel of light and speak words that resemble the truth, and I will lead him into battle and abandon him there, and so he will die." And the Lord said to him: "Go, and do so." That is why the apostle also says: "It is no great thing if Satan disguises himself as an angel of light, since his servants are disguised as well."

And so they deceive many by sight, word, or persuasion, using nothing else than what seems like the truth. When people choose, for a time, to believe words that seem genuine and sights that seem good and not evil, and to cling to them, they incur the inescapable sentence of eternal death, and after leaving the body they are ruined by various punishments and torments. This was the danger that came upon the king of the Jews at that time, because he chose to believe false prophets rather than the true prophets of God.

There is a heresy among the Jews who, after the death of Moses and the succession of Joshua son of Nun, worshipped Asthar and Astaroth and were handed over to captivity among the gentiles. For they worshipped Asthar and Astaroth, men and women, and their images. These were the names of kings of the Syrians and the Egyptians. Their sons and daughters were worshipped by their peoples, who afterwards also built temples for them. After their death, burying their descendants there as well, they gave them the names of gods and goddesses and offered sacrifices to them in the same way.

For there is the Astartium in Syria [?] and many other different ones. All this impiety blazed up at that time from the race of the Canaanites, which Moses, together with all his people, was commanded by the Lord to root out.

Others are the Herodians, so called after Herod, king of the Jews. They confess the resurrection and accept the law and the prophets, but they hope for and expect Herod, king of the Jews, who was struck down by an angel, as the Christ himself.

AFTER THE PASSION OF CHRIST OUR LORD AND HIS ASCENSION INTO HEAVEN there was a certain Simon Magus, a Samaritan by race, a Gittite, from a place so called, which is a village in Samaria. Given over to magic arts, he deceived many, saying that he was a certain power of God, a power which, he said, is above all powers.
The Samaritans revere him as a father and extol him as the founder of their pernicious heresy, and they strive to honour him with many praises.

He was baptized by the blessed apostles, but he departed from their faith and sowed a wicked and pernicious heresy. He said that he had been transformed only in appearance, that is, as if in a shadow, and that he had suffered in this way, though, he said, he did not really suffer.
He also dared to say that the world was made by angels, and that the angels were made by himself [?], endowed with certain thoughts from heaven, and that they deceived [?] the human race.

He asserts that there is also a certain other Thought, which descended into the world for the sake of human salvation: that Helen, he said, who is reported by the most foolish poets to have figured in the Trojan War.
And the powers which had made the world, he said, were led by desire for that Helen and stirred up strife. For she, he said, by arousing desire...

...desire in those powers and appearing in a woman's form, could not ascend into heaven, because the powers that were in heaven would not allow her to ascend. But she was waiting for another power, that is, the presence of Simon Magus himself, who would come and save her.

He also explains allegorically the wooden horse which the most foolish poets say was in the Trojan War, asserting that that device was the ignorance of all the impious nations. Yet it is well established that this Helen who was with the Magus was a prostitute from Tyre, that she followed this same Simon Magus, and that together with him she practised various kinds of magic and committed various crimes.

When he fled from the blessed apostle Peter out of the city of Jerusalem and came to Rome, and there contended with the blessed apostle before King Nero, he was utterly defeated by the prayer of the blessed apostle and struck down by an angel. So he deservedly perished, in such a way that his magic and his lies were made plain and exposed to all people.
After him came a certain man named Menander [?], who became his disciple and followed his impiety in everything.

After him a certain Saturninus, he too drawing from that source the kindling of a deadly doctrine, asserted that the world was made by angels, that the angels were distinct from that Power, that the world was divided up in order among the angels, and that they planned to make man.

So they made man, and man, he said, was their work. For a light was sent down from the supreme Power, which illuminated this world and drew the angels to desire, and then at once ascended into heaven.

But they, now longing for that light, desired to see its power; and since they could not, they said to one another: "Let us make man in our image and likeness." And when man had been made, since he was powerless, he could not be saved.
So the supreme Power, seeing what they had done, sent a spark, which set man right, raised him up, and made him live.
They hold, then, that the spark is saved, but suppose that everything else is given up and abandoned to those powers which made it.
They affirm that Christ appeared as a shadow and did not take true human flesh and a human soul, and that in this way he fulfilled the whole economy of the Saviour's mystery.

After these came Basilides [?], who is also called a heresiarch by many, because, while he set forth and spoke about the law, the prophets and the apostles, he thought otherwise and so violated the laws of Christian truth.

When he came to Egypt he taught, defining things thus: from the unbegotten and only God was born Mind; from Mind, the Word; from the Word, Understanding; from Understanding, Power and Wisdom; and from Power and Wisdom were made the Principalities and Powers and the various angels.

These angels, he said, made a heaven; after them other angels made a [second?] heaven; and so, produced one after another, others made a third heaven. And so in order, he said, still others made three hundred and sixty-five heavens.

He gives those powers the names of angels, and he himself, likewise given over to magic, deceives many ignorant people. He asserts that man was made by angels. Even the true almighty God he dares to call an angel, and says that he received the race of the Jews as his inheritance and led them out of the land of Egypt.

This one, then, he says, grew bolder and was lifted up against the other angels; and wishing to hold the others in subjection, he found the nations set against him, for the powers hostile to him stirred them up.

That is why, he says, various nations rose up against the Jews. He says that Christ suffered only in appearance, as if in a shadow. He also affirms that Simon of Cyrene went to the passion in his place. For it was he, he says, who carried the cross.

He also allows people to live wickedly and gives them licence to cling to worldly vices. He even forbids people to suffer martyrdom for the name of Christ the Lord, saying: "You do not know what you are longing for. For Christ did not suffer," he says, "nor was he crucified.
How then can you confess him as crucified," he says, "when he was not crucified, and you do not know who it was that suffered?"

Let us also see by what madness Nicolaus, the proselyte of Antioch, was deceived. He lived in the time of the apostles and was chosen by them as the seventh deacon, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles; but afterwards he departed from them and from sound doctrine and was ruined by various errors and deceptions.

He was at first with the apostles and with Stephen, the most blessed martyr. He too says that there are a great many powers; and from him arose chiefly the Gnostics, who think that they know something. These venerate Barbelo and a certain woman Nora,
others of them a certain Ialdabaoth, and others a man Caulacau. And setting out their doctrine, they say this:

In the beginning, they say, there was only darkness and the abyss and water, and from these a division was made in the middle, and the spirit separated these elements. Then the darkness, rushing upon the spirit, begot four Aeons, and these four begot another four Aeons.
And this right and left, they say, are light and darkness. They also say that a certain one lay with that woman and power, and from her were born gods and
men and angels and seven spirits of demons. They add also that certain prophets were born of her, one named Speciosus [?], and Barcabas.
Others, in their raving, put forward a Gospel of Perfection, and claim to see empty visions full of deceit and various dreams.

Others founded a heresy on Judas the betrayer, saying that Judas did a good work in betraying the Saviour. "For he," they say, "became for us the author of all good knowledge, and through him the heavenly mysteries were revealed to us.

For the powers in heaven," they say, "did not want Christ to suffer, knowing that if he suffered he would grant life to men; and Judas, knowing this—that if Christ suffered he would bring salvation to men—therefore betrayed the Saviour."

This wicked and impious claim sometimes seems almost plausible to certain empty and senseless people, though it is in every respect contrary to the truth and accursed, since the blessed prophet David beforehand and the Lord and Saviour himself condemned him, and the blessed apostles confirmed the Lord's sentence against him in their teaching.

After him there arose one named Carpocrates. He too spoke of one first principle, and from that principle, that is, from God, there came forth, he said, emanations of angels and powers; and the powers that are below made this visible creation in which, he said, we live.
He says that Christ was not born of the Virgin Mary and the divine Spirit, but holds that he was born a man from the seed of Joseph, and supposes that he was begotten by him carnally, like all men.
After his passion, he says, he was found to be better than others among the Jews in uprightness of life and conduct;
they proclaim that his soul was taken up into heaven, but reckon that his flesh was left behind on earth, and they hold that there is salvation of the soul [?] alone, but no salvation of the flesh.

Cerinthus succeeded to this man's error and to the likeness of his folly. He likewise taught about the birth of the Saviour and about the creation by angels, differing from him in nothing except that he agrees with the law in part, holding that it was given by God; and he considers the God of the Jews to be the very one who gave the law to the children of Israel.
He teaches circumcision and the keeping of the sabbath, and proclaims that Christ has not yet risen from the dead but will rise.

He does not accept the blessed apostle Paul; he honours Judas the betrayer; he accepts only the Gospel according to Matthew and spurns the other three gospels; he rejects the Acts of the Apostles; and he blasphemes the blessed martyrs.

In the time of the blessed apostles he stirred up a contentious dispute, saying that men must be circumcised. Because of this the blessed apostles, in their Acts, decreed a judgement against him and his heresy:

that those who came from the Gentiles and believed in Christ our Lord and Saviour need no longer submit to Judaism, that is, to circumcision and to other such carnal observances of empty superstition.
Ebion, the disciple of this Cerinthus, erring like him in many things, held that our Saviour was a man born carnally of Joseph, and taught that there was nothing divine in him; but

he asserted that he had the grace of God just as all the prophets had. He did not, however, believe him to be the God of majesty and the Son of God the Father, everlasting with the Father, although the divine Scriptures everywhere testify and proclaim him to be God everlasting with the true and everlasting Father.

After him there arose a certain Valentinus, a Pythagorean rather than a Christian, who belched out an empty and pernicious doctrine and preached a kind of arithmetic, that is, a most deceitful science of numbers, and so took captive the souls of many ignorant people. At first, indeed, he was in the Church.
But afterwards he grew proud and was deceived by no small error; and while living in the province of Cyprus he began to lay down the following:

In the beginning, he said, there was nothing else in the world but the Depth of the sea and Silence, which the foolish poets in their teaching call Chaos; and from this Depth and Silence came forth Mind and Truth; from Mind and Truth, the Word and Life; and from the Word and Life, Man and the Church;

from Man and the Church came forth twelve Aeons, that is, Ages; from the Word and Life came forth ten Aeons; and from Mind and Truth, eight Aeons; and this is the triacontad of Ages, that is, the thirty Aeons of Aeons. So he raves that the thirty Aeons are made up of the ogdoad, the decad and the dodecad.
He says that Christ was sent by the Father, whom he calls by the name of Depth, for the salvation of the whole world,

and that he brought his flesh down from heaven and received nothing from the holy Virgin, but passed through her, he affirms, like water through a channel. He therefore holds that the soul alone is saved, and that the human body is not saved.

There are others who succeeded him: Ptolemy, who brought in a doctrine equally empty, saying that there are four Aeons and another four, wishing to lay down some false invention newer than what his teacher Valentinus had fabricated.

After him a certain man named Secundus, likewise teaching about Aeons, asserts that they were made without number, and supposes that Christ appeared to the human race as a phantasm, that is, like a shadow, and did not have true human flesh.

After him there arose Heracleon, his disciple, saying that there is one first principle, whom he calls God; that from him another was then born; and from these two he asserts the generation of many principles, raving just like his teachers.

After him a certain Marcus, his successor, devising number and measure and calculation, and even a system of reckoning by letters, as though he were the discoverer of something plausible and new, and supposing that he could win praise from some, likewise fell into no small madness of error. For he says this:

There are twenty-four letters, he says, which contain the perfection of all things. For this reason, he says, Christ said: "I am the Alpha and the Omega." He also said that in the last time Christ descended upon Jesus in the form and likeness of a dove, and he taught that Christ himself was the dove, which

descended, he says, to the twelve Aeons, that is, to the twelve apostles; and he held that one of them fell, that is, Judas. He says that Christ appeared only in appearance and suffered as if in a shadow, and holds that he did not truly suffer in the body.

After him came Colorbasus [?], who likewise asserted that the life and generation of all people consist in letters and in the number of the elements and of the seven stars; and he did not recognize that the true salvation of mankind is to be hoped for in the majesty and power of Christ, or in his bodily presence.

After these there arose a certain Cerdo, who preached worse things than his teachers. When he came to Rome from Syria, he dared to say that there are two first principles, that is, one good god and one evil, and that the good god does good things and the evil one evil things.

He asserts that Jesus the Saviour was not born of the Virgin, did not appear in the flesh, and did not come down from heaven, but was seen by people only in appearance; he was not truly seen, he says, but was a shadow. Hence some thought he suffered, yet he did not truly suffer.

Marcion, his disciple, a native of Pontus from the city of Sinope, came to the city of Rome and, living there, sowed a wicked heresy. Questioning the holy presbyters of the catholic Church, he put before them the notions of his own deadly error, saying: "What is the meaning of what is written in the Gospel, where the Lord says:

'No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, nor new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the skins burst and the wine is spilled'? And again: 'There is no good tree that bears bad fruit, nor a bad tree that bears good fruit.'"
Receiving the interpretation of this from the holy presbyters, he did not submit to the truth, but instead reinforced the lie of his teacher Cerdo, likewise proclaiming one good god and one evil;
and he believed that Christ appeared only in appearance, that is, as if in a shadow, and that he suffered as a shadow, and not in true flesh.
He accepts only the Gospel according to Luke, not the other gospels, nor the epistles of the blessed apostle Paul, except those to Timothy and to Timothy [?];
for he passes over whatever the Scriptures say of Christ as of true God, and accepts only those passages that speak of him as of a man; nor does he confess that Christ is the judge of all.
Defeated and driven out of the city of Ephesus by blessed John the Evangelist and by the presbyters, he sowed this heresy at Rome.
After him a certain Lucan, laying down and decreeing things like Marcion's, lied in everything just as his teacher Marcion had.

Apelles was his disciple, preaching in some respects the same as Marcion. When some asked him what he believed about the faith, he answered: "I do not need to say, as Marcion does, that I assert two coeternal first principles;

for I proclaim that there is one first principle, whom I know as God. This God made the angels, and also made another power, whom I know to be a second god, who is also the power of God that made the world."

"But this god who made the world," he says, "is not good like the one who made him. He is subject to that God by whom he himself was made, and in all things obeys his will, his command and his precepts."
The Arians are now his partners and supporters, preaching and believing the same. He says that Christ appeared in the flesh, yet did not, as Valentinus held, bring his flesh down from heaven.
He also says that after the passion it was not flesh that rose, but that it was made of the four elements:

that is, he asserts that Christ took his body from the dry, the hot, the moist and the cold, and at the resurrection gave back to the elements what he had received from the world and let it go into the earth, while he himself ascended into heaven without flesh. These, then, in order, were the heresies in the time of the apostles.

AFTER THE PERSECUTION OF DECIUS there was a certain Tatian, a disciple of Saint Justin the martyr, who departed from the truth after Justin's martyrdom and despised in every respect the teaching of so great a saint, blessed martyr and master. He said that certain Aeons had been brought forth from heaven, and added this too, that Adam, our first-formed father, is not saved.
In proclaiming Aeons he raved like Marcion. He also abhors the begetting of children, rejects the lawful right of marriage, and does not confess that this right was established by God.

After these there arose others, the Cataphrygians, living in the province of Phrygia. They accept the prophets and the law, they confess the Father, the Son and the Spirit, and they await the resurrection of the flesh—all of which the catholic Church also proclaims;
but they announce certain prophets of their own, namely one named Montanus, and Priscilla and Maximilla, whom neither the prophets nor Christ foretold.

They add that the fullness of the Holy Spirit was not granted through the blessed apostles by the gift of Christ, but suppose that it was imparted through those false prophets of theirs; and they separate themselves from the catholic Church on account of those false prophets and false teachers of theirs.

They baptize the dead and celebrate their mysteries in public. They call Pepuza, their village in Phrygia, by the name Jerusalem; there Maximilla and Priscilla and Montanus himself are known to have spent their vain and fruitless lives.

There too the "cynic" [?] mystery and an accursed impiety involving an infant are celebrated. For it is said that at Easter they mix an infant's blood into their sacrifice, and so send it everywhere to their pernicious and false followers.
After these a certain Theodotus, a Byzantine by birth, denied Christ our God and Saviour during a persecution, and he began to say, teaching thus: "Christ was an ordinary man, like all men."

He said this so that he would no longer suffer from people the reproach of having denied, reasoning that if anyone said to him, "Why did you deny Christ, God and Lord?" he could say: "I denied a man, not God."

These people use the passages of Scripture that speak of Christ as of a man, but those that speak of him as God they do not accept, reading them yet in no way understanding them, and so showing themselves partners in pagan impiety and Jewish blindness rather than sharers in Christian salvation.

There are others who speak of metangismos, that is, that the Son enters into the Father and is in him like a vessel within a vessel. They do not know what they are asserting, since the Saviour did not say that the Son enters into the Father, but taught [?] his equality in divinity and power, not an entering in or a being contained, as these people madly hold,
not understanding that as the Father is immeasurable, so too is the Son, and so too is the Holy Spirit, equal in all things,

so that the Trinity is unchangeable, immeasurable, almighty and everlasting everywhere, as is proclaimed to us most plainly from the holy Scriptures: there are three Persons living forever and equal in all majesty and power, yet the Son and the Holy Spirit are properly from the Father.

After these, others who broke away from them said similar things, and they add that Melchizedek the priest is the great power of God; and they assert certain various names of men, at odds with the catholic faith.

Others are the Noetians [?], named after a certain senseless man called Noetus, who said that the Father almighty is himself Christ, and that he himself was born, he himself suffered, and he himself died in the body. He also said that he himself was Moses, and that his brother was the prophet Elijah.

After him Sabellius of Libya, his disciple, likewise followed his teacher's likeness and error; from him they were afterwards called Sabellians. They are also called Patripassians, and Praxeans after Praxeas and Hermogenes, who were in Africa; and these, holding such views, were cast out of the catholic Church.

What is this folly of the Galatians, the heretics Seleucus and Hermias? While they hold that God is incorporeal, they also assert that hyle, that is, the matter of the world, is coeternal with God. And the matter of the elements—which is without soul and therefore irrational,

and which was made by God the Father through the Son out of nothing, so that what did not exist before might exist—they do not accept in this way. They say, moreover, that the spirit of man, that is, the soul, was not made by God through the Son but comes from the earth;

and they assert that evil is sometimes from God and sometimes from matter. They deny that the Saviour sits in the flesh at the right hand of the Father, and think that he stripped off his flesh and placed it in the sun, because the prophet said—though they do not know what he meant—"In the sun he has set his tabernacle."

Following Plato, these too, slaves to vanities, deny a visible paradise and think that human souls are made of fire and spirit. They do not use baptism, because of the saying of blessed John the Baptist: "He will baptize you in the Spirit and fire."

They say that angels, not Christ the Saviour, are the creators of our souls. They assert that this world is hell, and they proclaim that the resurrection is the procreation of children which takes place daily in the human race; they do not look for and proclaim that future resurrection of immortality and glory.

There are others, disciples of these, who are called Proclianites and Hermeonites. They add various further errors. They teach about what is written in the prophet Ezekiel concerning the four living creatures: they think that the lion stands for the king of the Parthians, the calf for the Egyptians, the eagle for the Romans, and the man for the most pious.

They use the book of Wisdom of that Sirach who wrote a single book of Wisdom after Solomon, that is, a long time after him. But they deny that Christ came in the flesh, they do not hope for the resurrection and the judgment, and they do not believe that he was born of a virgin.

They live in parts of Galatia, and like foxes lying in hiding they prey on a great many people, as Solomon testified when he said: Catch for us the little foxes that ruin the vineyards of the Lord the Saviour.

There are others who are called Florians or Carpocratians, and who are also called Soldiers, because they came from among the military. They deny the judgment and the resurrection and do not believe that Christ was born of a virgin. They think that the whole resurrection consists in begetting children through wicked intercourse, so that in their church, after sunset and with the lamps put out, they did not hesitate to have intercourse with the women, thinking that they were fulfilling the precept of the law:

Be born and multiply. They hasten to obey a wicked Judaism and paganism rather than to assent to Christian truth, and they cling instead to the life and the madness of cattle. Scripture, too, compared them to the life of cattle.

There are others who are in doubt about the most saving day of Easter. They maintain that Easter is to be celebrated on the fourteenth day of the moon, not as the catholic Church celebrates it, and they maintain that it must always be celebrated in the month of March.
In doing this they do not always keep Sunday as the day of Easter. They do not reckon the hours and days, but celebrate on the second, third, fourth, fifth or sixth day of the week.

By this error they fail to recognize the one true and saving day of the Easter of our Lord, established and confirmed for the whole world by the Lord through the course of the moon, its numbering, the months and the intercalations. Since they do not reckon these things, they do not know what they are celebrating.

Another heresy is that of the Chiliasts, that is, of the thousand years. It teaches as follows: When Christ comes from heaven, it says, those thousand years will be ours to live once again in the flesh, to beget and to eat, as happens daily now in this world. They know nothing of the heavenly food, that is, the food of immortality.
[?] that that reward will come, not this perishable and passing one, since the Lord too in the Gospel, to certain Jews who supposed this, [said:]

You do not know the Scriptures, he said, and you are ignorant of their power: for on the day of judgment they will neither marry nor be given in marriage, but will be like the angels. And again the apostle says: The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, peace, and everlasting joy in the Spirit of the Lord.

After these there are other heretics, who do not accept the Gospel according to John or his Apocalypse. Since they do not understand the power of Scripture and have no desire to learn, they remain in heresy and perish,

so that they even dare to say that [the Gospel] is by that heretic Cerinthus [?], and likewise that the Apocalypse is not by blessed John the evangelist and apostle but by the heretic Cerinthus, who was exposed as a heretic by the blessed apostles at that time and cast out of the Church.
After these the Manichees arose from Persia, from a man named Manes, or Turbo as he was also called. They took their pernicious kindling from those
earlier heretics. They maintain that there are two gods, one good and one evil, and they preach that there is a war between god and god. They think that the soul of man comes properly from God,

but they hold that the body was made by the devil. They deny the resurrection, they do not hope for the judgment, they worship demons, they adore the elements, and like pagans they call on the names of gods and goddesses. They teach that there are certain man-women who share in both natures, and they are slaves to wicked depravity.

They were defeated in debate by the holy bishop Archelaus, cast out and branded, and exposed to everyone at that time. Yet like robbers, under the guise of professing Christianity, they still do not cease to take captive the souls of many by lies and by a beastly depravity.
They are said to be hiding in Spain and in the Five Provinces, and to take many captive every day by this deceit.
There are others, the Patricians, named after a certain Patricius who lived in the city of Rome. They maintain that man's flesh was not made by God, but they think it was made by the devil.
They also decree that it is to be despised and rejected in every way, so that some of them have not even hesitated to take their own lives of their own accord.
Others, the Symmachians, disciples of this man, think the same in every respect. They do not hope for the judgment, and they preach that one should be a slave to worldly vices and fleshly desires.

After these there was a certain Paul of Samosata in Syria, who denied that the Word of God, that is, Christ, God, the Son of God, is substantial and personal and eternal with the Father. He said instead that the Word was uttered, that is, like a kind of air, and taught that it was not to be believed as the living person of the Son, eternal with the eternal Father.

He preached Christ as a righteous man, not as true God. He was rather a Judaizer, and he also taught circumcision; and so it was he who at that time taught a certain Zenobia, a queen in the East, to Judaize.
After him Photinus followed his teaching in everything and preached the same. Persisting in this lie, he was defeated by the holy bishops and expelled from the church of the city of Sirmium.

THERE ARE THE ARIANS, named after Arius, a presbyter of the city of Alexandria, who lived under Alexander, the bishop of good memory, and under the holy emperor Constantine of good memory. He said that the Son of God is like God;

but by saying he was like him in name only, and not believing that he was from the very divine substance of the Father, he fell into a dangerous heresy. For a creature too is said to be like God, since Scripture says: Let us make man in our image and likeness.

Yet neither man nor angel is properly and by nature from God, that is, begotten of that ineffable and eternal divine substance of the Father, as the only Son is, who was properly begotten of the Father and is eternal. Man and angel were made out of nothing.

But since the Son is true, he must be acknowledged as begotten of that divine substance of the Father. For the only Son cannot be true God in any other way than by being properly begotten of that divine substance of the Father.

The eternal likeness of the Son, then, is according to his works: as the Father acts, so the Son likewise does all things, being begotten of the divine substance of that same nature, because he was properly born of him and is eternal, not made out of nothing like man and angel or any other creature, which is perishable in every respect.

There are others, the Semi-Arians. They think rightly about the Father and the Son, believing that there is one substance of the same nature and one divinity; but they preach that the Spirit is not of the divine substance and not true God,

but a Spirit made and created, so that they join him with creation and put him on a level with it. Yet Christ the Lord joined him to the Father and to himself in the faith of the baptism of eternal salvation, commanded that he be worshipped by all believers together with the Father and the Son, and ordained that he be preached as true God in every age. They do not understand that when the evangelist says:
All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made, he is not speaking of the Holy Spirit, as though the Spirit were made through the Son.

For the prophet declares that the Trinity made all things visible and invisible, when he says: By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the Spirit of his mouth. So in the whole of creation, which was made through the Spirit, he left out nothing that was not made through him.

Otherwise, in the faith, the servant would not be joined with the Lord, if the divine and Holy Spirit were a creature. For this reason the whole of Scripture, and the Lord by a heavenly sentence, had declared that all sins are forgiven to men except blasphemy against the divine and adorable Spirit.

After these come the Eunomians, named after Eunomius, a disciple of Arius, enemies of the true faith in everything. They say that there are three substances of different nature, like gold, silver and bronze; that the Father made the Son, and that the Son in turn, who is a creature, made the Holy Spirit, as they put it.

They maintain that the Son is not like the Father, because he is a creature, and that the Spirit is not like the Son, because he was made by the Son. Quite openly they side with pagan impiety and Jewish wickedness rather than choosing to obey Christian doctrine and the catholic faith.
There are others who go astray about the incarnation. They say that the Saviour did not take on a true rational human soul, but only a human body. And by taking the soul away from the
body, they deny the true salvation of man. How then can the soul be said [to be saved] if it was not taken on by the Saviour? Yet the Saviour says: My soul is sorrowful even unto death.

Otherwise it could not have been called a soul unless it were in him who had come for its [?] sake. So both of these were in the Saviour's incarnation, that is, the body and the soul, which he deigned to take on for our salvation.
We should know that he had a true human soul, possessing understanding, and a human body with bodily feeling likewise, so that he could suffer pain in the body and die.

Yet this flesh is known to have been made of the Holy Spirit, and the soul, of course, to have been created, as it is written in the Gospel: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. And that he had a true soul [?], saying: I lay down my soul for you.

And concerning his flesh, capable of suffering, he said to Thomas: [?] for a spirit does not have bones and flesh, as you see that I have. And the blessed apostle Peter bore witness about the Saviour, saying: His soul was not abandoned to hell, nor did his flesh see corruption.
And in that he became incarnate, he is believed, known, worshipped and preached in the catholic Church as both man, for the sake of our salvation, and true God.

There are others, the Tropites, who say that the Word was changed into flesh. They do not understand what the blessed apostle John says: The Word became flesh and dwelt among us. They do not pay heed to the fact that the Word, that is, God the Son of God, is unchangeable and cannot be altered; but the flesh which he took for our salvation he himself formed, assumed and put on because of our incapacity.

So these things, joined into one for our salvation so that he might be seen, declared not a change of the Word into flesh but rather the assumption of a visible reality, so that the invisible one might be seen through visible flesh, believed and known, and worshipped by the human race in a way it could grasp.

There are other heretics who go astray about the passion. They say that in the passion our Lord Christ put off the flesh and so ascended into heaven, and that divinity is no longer in it, as they put it.

For, they say, he neither rose in the flesh after the passion nor ascended into heaven with the flesh. Yet the whole salvation of man consists, beyond any doubt for us and for all believers, in the passion of his flesh, in its resurrection and in its ascension into heaven;
for the blessed angels also told the apostles in the Acts of the Apostles, for our faith and joy: As you have seen him ascending into heaven, so hope for him to come again from heaven.

There are others, the Aerians, so called after a certain Aerius. They devote themselves to abstinence, and a great many of them live in the province of Pamphylia. They are also called Encratites, that is, the abstinent.
They own nothing, and they abhor foods which God gave to the human race with his blessing. They also condemn marriage, which comes from the law, maintaining that it was not instituted by God.

Another heresy is that of the Borborians, who are entangled in the vices of the world and slaves to evil desires. They do not hope for the judgment to come, but instead praise the fleshly desire of the world.
So they go into the mud and, smeared with it, disfigure their faces and limbs, displaying them to everyone as though God's creation were to be blamed,
whereas that whirlpool of faults and vices, that ruinous damnation, came down from the will of men, not by the permission of the divine law.
There are others in Galatia named Artotyrites, who offer bread and cheese, not what the catholic and apostolic Church celebrates in its offering.

There are others again in Galatia, the Ascodrugites, who inflate a wineskin, set it down and cover it in their church, and go around it, raving and revelling like those pagan worshippers of Father Liber, frenzied in their insane minds after the manner of the heathen. They do not understand what the Saviour said: that new wineskins must be taken, and new wine put into them, not into old ones.

And as they hasten to serve their own blindness, they are found to be strangers in every way to Christian salvation. For the apostle casts down that Jewish justification and fleshly vanity, but confirms the true and complete judgment of Christ, saying: The old things have passed away; behold, all things have been made new through Christ.

For the Lord was speaking of the law and the shadow, and of his own grace of fullness, and of the two men [?], as the apostle says: The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly.
What existed in shadow, and what was to come, greater and better, in the Lord's presence, this he announced by teaching and confirmed by the witness of deeds.
There are others, the Passalorynchites, who put a finger to their nostrils, mouths and lips as if constantly practising silence, devoting their zeal, as it were, to nothing else but keeping quiet.
In doing this they wish to imitate the blessed prophets, as it were, because blessed David says: Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth, and a door to enclose my lips.

And because the blessed prophets, devoting themselves to fasting, often kept silence, these people have appropriated this and think they are observing something. They hasten to follow the vanity of Pythagoras rather than the heavenly life and wisdom of the prophets.
There are others, so called the Aquarians, who offer water in the heavenly sacraments, not what the catholic and apostolic Church is accustomed to do.

There are other heretics who claim that there are prophets every day and preach that prophecies still take place. They do not know that the law and the prophets lasted until blessed John the Baptist, and that the end of the law and the prophets was fulfilled and completed in the presence of Christ.

There are others, the Colluthians, named after a certain Colluthus in Egypt, who say that God is not the maker of evils. Another man, on the contrary, opposed him by saying that God is the maker of evils; he too was likewise a heretic. And while both were carried away by a futile dispute, they did not know the force of the argument.

For Scripture proclaimed that God makes good things and none the less also makes evils, since the prophet says: I am the Lord, who make peace and create evils. And another prophet says: Is there evil in a city which God has not done?

But Scripture did not say that these evils were made by God by nature, but because of causes that arose, namely from men who sin against the Lord under the law. These are the trials, persecutions and various afflictions which, by God's permission, rise up against sinners, as it is written: Who gave Israel up to plunder? Was it not the Lord, against whom they sinned and in whose ways they would not walk?

But nowhere does Scripture say that God made evils by nature. For it says in the book of Genesis: Behold, all the things that God made were very good, that is, the creatures of the world. And elsewhere the prophet says: For God did not make evil, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living.

Since, then, evils exist not by nature because of God the creator, but because of the will of men, which, being subject to God's law, is pressed by judgment and held in check by correction, these things are brought upon men daily by the Lord for the sake of their conversion. When, therefore,

these things are said, people do not understand how they were meant. For the evils imposed on men as correction are full of instruction and benefit, and the perverse will of men deserves to suffer them, as the apostle says: Is God unjust, who inflicts his wrath on men?

Yet all these things are not permitted to befall the human race without benefit and future gain. For the righteous man, by enduring tribulation, is proved more faithful and more righteous; while the sinner either is corrected and stops sinning, or, if he persists, is taken from the world, so that he may not sin further while living in the body.

So either he is corrected while he still remains in the body and will no longer delay doing good works, or his mind is summoned away so that he may cease from sin, as the apostle says: He who has died is justified from sin.

Another heresy says that the world is not changed but always remains in the same state, even after the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ from heaven, although he himself says: All things will pass away and be changed.

They do not understand that the Lord said this about the changing of the elements, so that once these are changed a new creation may be formed. David teaches this too: They will perish, he says, but you are for ever. And the Lord says: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.

And: I will make a new heaven and a new earth, says the Lord. He therefore announces that the elements are to be restored rather than to perish, even though it is not impossible for God, who made all things out of nothing, to destroy all things again, as most blessed Job says:

But if he destroys everything, who will say to him, What have you done? If, then, you think this way, you acknowledge the almighty power of the Lord Christ; or if someone thinks that they are to be restored, he understands consistently. For even if Scripture shows the seeds as perishing, that is, that the world itself can come to nothing, yet [?] because what he made does not perish.

For, as Solomon says, he made all things out of nothing, so that the things that were not might be. And in the resurrection of men Scripture shows the seeds not as perishing but as coming to greater glory, as the apostle says: It is sown a natural body, it rises a spiritual body; it is sown in corruption, it rises in incorruption. And again the same most blessed apostle says:

For the expectation of the creation waits for the revelation of the children of God; for the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope of the glory of future dignity. Therefore, he says, the creation itself will also be set free from the bondage of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the children of God. He thus shows that the elements will advance to the glory of the children of God, that is, human beings together with this very visible creation, since the Lord says:
Then the sun will shine sevenfold. So the elements will pass over to a greater glory and remain in it together with human beings, although the Lord who made all things can also bring them to nothing.

But the surpassing majesty and power of Christ lies in this: that he promises that these same elements will pass over to greater glory. For the apostle too both announces and prophesies that these elements will melt and come to nothing.

Another heresy maintains that people ought to walk barefoot, because, it says, it was said to Moses: Take off your shoes, and because blessed Isaiah walked in this way for three years. But these things belong rather to human and vain superstition, not to the tradition of the saints or to the command, authority and power of our Lord Jesus Christ.
THE NOVATIANS AROSE AFTER THE LAST PERSECUTION, from a certain Novatus. Before this they believed as the catholic Church does, accepting the Old and New Testaments.
But because many of the faithful lapsed during the persecution and were received back to penance by the catholic Church, they grew angry, or rather were led by presumption and

pride, and tried to sow a vain doctrine. They separated themselves from the catholic Church and were out of harmony with the goodness and mercy of Christ, saying that there is no room for penance for a believer after baptism. They do not know what he cries out through the prophet: As I live, says the Lord,

do I desire the death of the sinner, and not rather that he turn back and live? If they say that Scripture said this of those who are to be baptized and not of the faithful, let them hear the Saviour, after the baptism of water, speaking of another baptism, namely the baptism of penance through suffering. He speaks thus: I have a baptism,

he says, to be baptized with, and how I hasten, if only you knew! He shows us plainly that after the baptism which he had given earlier through water, another baptism too, of suffering and penance, is to be granted by his goodness and mercy to those of the human race who fall, and bestowed by that same Lord.

The apostles, understanding this about his most saving passion, preached that after that first grace he had also conferred this on the human race. For as one who provides for all and is almighty, he grants even to sinners through penance that whoever has fallen, rising up and fighting again and persevering in it, may hope to obtain from the Lord the victory to be desired.

For in Christ his mercy, justice and goodness abound daily for the sake of those who sin and repent. So blessed Paul grieved over those who had not done penance for their sin, as he said in his epistle: Who is weak, and I am not weak? And again: Lest when I come to you the Lord humble me again because of some who have not done penance. And the blessed apostle Peter had said to Simon the magician:

Do penance, if perhaps what you have done may be forgiven you. And Paul ordered that the man he had cast out be received back again after a time. Such people, then, may suffer loss of rank, but not loss of salvation, as the Lord says: There are many dwellings with my Father.

There are others, the Montenses, who rebaptize any people they have led astray, and in their madness promise a baptism of their own over and above the baptism of the catholic church. They are also called Donatians, after a certain Donatus who lived in Africa and sowed this heresy. They are now also called Parmenians, after a certain Parmenian who recently took over their errors and falsehood.

There are others in Gaul, Spain and Aquitaine who are abstainers, so to speak. They follow a most pernicious fragment of the Gnostics and Manichees alike and do not hesitate to preach the same things. By their persuasion they separate married people, and they promise abstinence from foods. Yet such a grace was granted by Christ, not by a precept of the law,
but to human free will, for the sake of heavenly advancement and dignity. For the Lord says to Peter: "Not everyone accepts this word." And again the same Lord says:

"Whoever puts away his wife except on the ground of a crime makes her commit adultery." So it is one thing for this to be done by common consent, in order to obtain greater praise from the Lord, and another to urge it against the law and act against the will of both.

And again: "Let the one who does not eat not despise the one who eats, and let the one who eats not judge the one who does not eat." What comes from free will, then, deserves praise. Indeed, it is rather a desire for a fuller heavenly reward.
But what is outside the law was not handed down by God Christ. It was invented by the empty presumption and error of men. For it is written: "I have given you all things to eat, like grass."

They do this so that, by gradually despising foods, they may say that foods are not good, and so assert that they were not granted to men by God as food but were made by the devil. This is what they think, and on this basis they now strive to preach that creation was not created by God but made by the devil. By this lie they have taken the souls of many captive.

There are others in Africa who are called Circuitors. They go about the land and force those they find on the road to kill them, saying that they long to suffer martyrdom. Under this pretext many of them sometimes turn to robbery.

Some of them die like the biothanati, those who meet a violent end, by throwing themselves off a cliff, and they undergo various kinds of ruinous death. Since they hurry to perish in this way without cause, they suffer the loss of an honourable death, and they entangle themselves before God's future judgment rather than set themselves free.

There are others who will not take food with other people. They are led by empty presumption, thinking that they are doing something better because, they say, the prophets also did this. They do not know that a different dispensation was established for men by the ordering of Christ the Lord. These think rightly about the Father and the Son, but they do not understand the Spirit rightly. They believe that the Holy Spirit is created and made and is not God, as the scriptures proclaim and the catholic church preaches.

Another heresy asserts that we ought to keep Easter together with the Jews. These people live in Galatia, Syria, Phrygia and Jerusalem. Since they follow the Jews, they perish in error together with them.

In this the Jews also confirm their own lie, when they see certain unlearned Christians following the vanity of their law rather than the rule of catholic truth. And these people celebrate together with them all the same, so that they are revealed and recognized by everyone as sharers in the crime and wickedness of the Jews.

Another heresy holds only the apocrypha, that is, the secret writings, of the prophets and apostles. It does not accept the canonical scriptures, that is, the law and the prophets, namely the Old and New Testaments.

Since they want to read only those apocrypha, and read them diligently, they hold views contrary to the canonical scriptures. Little by little they lay down doctrines and pronounce opinions against those scriptures, setting down decrees against the law and the prophets and against the ordinances of the most blessed apostles.

Chief among these are the Manichees, Gnostics, Nicolaitans and Valentinians, and very many others. They have the apocrypha of the prophets and apostles, that is, separate Acts, and they disdain to read the canonical scriptures.

For this reason the apostles' blessed successors established that nothing else should be read in the catholic church except the law and the prophets and the gospels, the Acts of the Apostles and the thirteen epistles of Paul, and seven others: two of Peter, three of John, one of Jude and one of James. These seven are joined to the Acts of the Apostles.

The hidden scriptures, that is, the apocrypha, may be read by the perfect for the sake of morals, but they should not be read by everyone. The heretics did not understand them, and they added many things and took away whatever they wished.

For the Manichees have the apocrypha of blessed Andrew the apostle, that is, the Acts he performed when he came from Pontus into Greece [?], which the disciples who were then following the blessed apostle wrote down. So the Manichees and others like them have the Acts of blessed Andrew, and of blessed John the evangelist, and likewise of Peter the most blessed apostle, and also of Paul the blessed apostle.

In these Acts the apostles performed great signs and wonders, so that even cattle, dogs and wild beasts spoke. Because of this the lost heretics have also held that human souls are like those of dogs and cattle.

There are others who do not accept that the epistle of blessed Paul to the Hebrews is his. They say instead that it belongs either to Barnabas the blessed apostle or to Clement, bishop of the city of Rome.

Others say it is by Luke, the most blessed evangelist. Some also wish to read the epistle the blessed apostle wrote to the Laodiceans. But people of unsound views have added certain things to it, so it is not read in church. Even if some people read it, only his thirteen epistles, and sometimes the epistle to the Hebrews, are read to the people in church.

Because he wrote the epistle to the Hebrews rhetorically, in a pleasing style, they do not think it belongs to the same apostle. And because it also says that Christ was made, it is not read. The same goes for what it says about repentance, because of the Novatians.

When he says that Christ was made, he means with respect to the body. He did not say that he was made in his divinity, for in the same place he teaches that the Son is of the divine substance of the Father: "Who is," he says, "the brightness of glory and the image of his substance."

Nor does his teaching exclude repentance. Rather, it shows a different degree of dignity between the one who kept himself whole and the one who sinned. So the one who sinned suffers a loss of dignity, not the forfeiture of salvation.
For if someone fights bravely through martyrdom, he will recover his former health. Or if he lives worthily in this world, he obtains what he desires to attain.
In that epistle he excludes the rebaptizers. He does not deny that the baptism of repentance should be conferred, even though it will sometimes be found fruitless in many penitents,

while others have afterwards been commended by the Lord even in this world for their faith, life and good works, persevering now in good things and fruitful works. As the Lord had said through the prophet: "I will not remember his evil deeds, but rather his good ones, if he now remains in good works."

The Meletians are others, named after a certain Meletius in Egypt. He had belonged to the Arian party and was cast out by the catholic church. Afterwards, as though he were following the truth, he was received back, and his disciples together with him.

But after this they again chose to act without distinction, and they held communion both with heretics and with the catholic church. When the catholic church learned of their indifference, it shut them out of its communion.

There are others in Egypt and Alexandria, named after a certain Rhetorius. He praised all heresies, saying that they all thought rightly, that none of them erred, and that they all walked rightly. He did not think they believed wrongly. If he praised everyone, then, whom did he censure?

So he does not hold what is true. On his view, Photinus too must be praised, a heretic who denies that Christ is God with the Father before the ages, along with every heresy that blasphemes against the Father, the Son or the Spirit.

Why should he praise blasphemous heretics, when Christ the Lord has already condemned them from this present world? For he said that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is not forgiven to those who blaspheme and persist in it, neither here nor in the age to come. So it is clear that this man too is a heretic, or rather knows nothing at all, since he judged that such people should be praised instead of being censured and cast out.

Another heresy says that the divinity felt pain when the flesh, joined to the divinity, suffered on the cross. They are wrong. By nature the divinity cannot suffer, be held or be seen, and neither can the human soul, which was made by God. As the Lord says:

"Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Fear rather the one who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna." So those who say that Christ's divinity is by nature capable of suffering are wrong in every way, and it is impious of them to think that it felt pain, or wept, or groaned. Christ's passion belongs to the flesh. It was the flesh that by nature felt pain, not the divinity.

That is why the Jews did not recognize him as he spoke in flesh capable of suffering. Yet the law and the prophets had proclaimed him to them as true God, and had openly preached that he would come in the flesh. As the prophet says: "God will come openly." And again the same prophet David: "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup." What is the cup but his passion?

Though he conferred so great a gift of goodness and mercy on the human race, the most wicked people of the Jews did not know him. So he suffered in flesh capable of suffering, not in his divinity, which by nature cannot suffer. He is acknowledged and believed in this way. Yet the divinity was not absent: it was joined with the body throughout, because of the mystery of fulfilment that had been decreed and determined beforehand.

The apostle knew this and did not separate the divinity from the flesh on the cross, saying: "For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty." So blessed Paul joined the two, to show us the fullest goodness and mercy of Christ. Blessed Peter the apostle, on the other hand, taught openly what by nature can suffer and what cannot, saying: "He died indeed in the body, but was made alive in the spirit."

So the flesh was not absent from the divinity, nor the divinity from the flesh, when the human flesh suffered according to its nature. In this very event, by the permission of Christ's divinity, the Lord was fulfilling the mystery for the sake of our salvation, so that the enemy might be utterly defeated. He who was God in the flesh was seen to suffer as a man, so that he might conquer the enemy, not for himself but for us. We had been defeated before, but through his passion he would open to those who believe in him the power to conquer, and grant heavenly glory to those who follow him.

So God did not undergo any natural suffering, and no such pain arose in his divinity, as some suppose. Otherwise he would have been man only, not God and man, as it is written. Rather, the mystery of our eternal salvation was being fulfilled, which the law and the prophets alike had announced beforehand.

Another heresy says that God is three-formed, so to speak, and composite: one part belongs to the Father, another to the Son, another to the Holy Spirit. They assert that this is what must be believed, and in saying so they neither know nor understand the meaning of divine scripture.

By speaking of a kind of three-formed substance, they blaspheme worse than many others. They do not know that the one who sent is one, and the one who was sent is another. There is the true person of the Father, who sent the Son. There is the true person of the Son, who came from the Father.
