And there is the true person of the Spirit, who was sent from the Son and the Father.

These three persons have one truth, an equal majesty and substance, and an everlasting divinity. The person of the Father is immeasurable and beyond words, and so is the person of the Son, and so is that of the Holy Spirit. In the distinction of names and of the three persons, then, there is no difference of nature.
So this Trinity is immeasurable, invisible and beyond words. It is known by faith alone, and it cannot be worthily expressed by the explanation of a human voice or by mortal sense.

When scripture says that the Father sends the Son and the Son sends the Holy Spirit, it speaks this way for the sake of the persons. It does not show them divided by separation of place. It speaks this way because of the heretics Sabellius and Photinus, who refused to think worthily about God. As the Lord says: "To whom do you liken me, says the Lord, and to whom shall I be like? [?] For as heaven is distant from the earth, so far are your senses, thoughts and counsels from my senses and thoughts, says the Lord."

So when scripture says that the Father sent and that the Son was sent, it speaks for the sake of the persons, so that no one should suppose either that the Father himself was sent or that the Son himself sent [?]. Sabellius raves on this point because he does not understand it so. And again, so that no one would think the Son, sent from heaven, was not everywhere with the Father, he did say that he was sent by the Father, yet he showed that he is everywhere with the Father, saying: "The Father who sent me is with me."

So he did not mean a separation of place, since the Son himself fills and contains all things together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. He deigned to teach these things in this way so that we may believe the person of the Father to be true, the person of the Son to be such as the Father's, and the person of the Holy Spirit to be true like the Son's, and so that we may recognize that these three persons share one substance of quality, majesty and power.

Above all when he was placed in the flesh, he deigned to act and speak in this way for our salvation, so that we may be able in some measure to know, grasp and understand something about God. In the flesh his humility shone out to the world, and his goodness, which is beyond words, and his condescension to human frailty shone forth with mercy and generosity so abundant that they were made plain to the human race.

Another heresy is uncertain about the number of the heavens. Scripture declares that on the first day heaven and earth were made, these two elements, and that on the second day the firmament of water was made. And it testifies that this firmament too was called heaven.

David, for his part, speaks of the heavens this way: "Praise the Lord God of the heaven of heavens, and the waters that are above the heavens." So if anyone wishes to accept six heavens, following David, with this firmament as the seventh, he does not err. For Solomon speaks of three heavens this way: "Heaven and the heaven of heaven."

Blessed Paul the apostle likewise declares that he was caught up to the third heaven. So whether someone accepts seven heavens, like blessed David, or three, or two, he does not err, for the Lord also says: "Father who is in the heavens."

Even the most foolish pagans sometimes profess one heaven and a pole. So blessed David taught the full truth, while Solomon taught part of it, and blessed Paul likewise. The book of Genesis has told us of two heavens.

Another heresy is uncertain about the earth. It says that this earth is the only one and that there is no other. It does not know that there is another, which is like the womb of all things and contains the whole universe. In scripture it appears as hyle, that is, matter, which is invisible and unformed and was made by God on the first day.
The earth we live in is shown to be founded upon the water, as David said: "You who founded the earth upon the water."

For that earlier earth, the womb of all things, made on the first day, is immense. It contains the water and this earth that we inhabit. At the command of Christ the Lord and Saviour, this earth yields crops and fruits in abundance to the human race, to birds, reptiles, cattle and all other creatures, as it is written in the book of Genesis, that is, of creation.

Another heresy is uncertain about water. Its followers assert that water was not made by God but has always existed of itself. They do not know that if the greater element, earth, was made, then all the more was the lesser one, water, which is contained by the earth. As the prophet Jonah says: "I am a servant of God, who made the sea and the land."

David likewise says that water was made by the Lord, and so do the three young men. So the earth that contains all things is one, and the earth founded upon the water is another. The second is this earth that we inhabit, of which the prophet says: "You who founded the earth upon the water." [?] It is certainly not that first earth.

It is this earth, then, that must be renewed and purified. We know that it is often shaken by earthquakes, and of it the Lord says: "I make a new heaven and a new earth." And again, in the gospel, the Lord says that heaven and earth will pass away.
This earth, then, is known to draw its substance from the roots, as it were, of that earlier earth. It was commanded to stand above the water, and it provides food in abundance for the human race.

Another heresy says that man's body was made first, not the soul, and that the body, not man's soul, is the image of God. Its followers think that the Lord spoke in terms of predestination, since scripture says: "And God made man; in his own image he made him; male and female he made them." They do not know what the prophet meant.

When he says, "Let us make," he promises that he will make. When he says, "God made," he shows that the work has already been done, and he has declared that what was made was not the flesh but the soul, which is rational.

There is no doubt that flesh without a soul cannot speak, so the flesh is the instrument of the soul, which is a rational thing. When scripture first says that male and female were made, it is not referring to the sex of bodies. It is pointing to the soul that rules and the soul that is subject.

Some foolish people suppose that bodies were made first and lay lifeless, but it is clear that this is not so, since the flesh of Adam and of the woman was made afterwards. For on the seventh day scripture speaks of Adam this way: "And the Lord took earth from the clay and formed the man whom he had made."

You see, then, how scripture first shows that man was made, that is, the soul, rational and immortal and created by the Lord, which is rightly called the image of God. Then it showed that the earth taken from the clay was joined to the soul, that is, that the outer man, the fragile body, was formed on the following day. And so scripture testifies and proclaims that a deep sleep was sent upon Adam, and that afterwards the Lord took from his rib and made the woman.

There is no doubt that the soul was made first, on the sixth day, and that on the seventh day Adam's body was formed from the earth, and that scripture then showed the woman made from the man's body, that is, from his side. The evident account of the truth is this: the soul was made first and the flesh formed afterwards, and then, at the end, spiritual grace was bestowed by God's inbreathing, so that the Lord might show man now capable of the divine law and not powerless. Blessed David also said that the soul was made
first, and then the body was formed: "Your hands," he says, "made and fashioned me." And he declared that the Spirit was poured in afterwards, saying: "And do not take your Holy Spirit from me."

Another heresy says that the inbreathing is the soul, and not that an inbreathing was given into the soul. Its followers do not see that if the inbreathing is the soul, there is no way to tell what was properly breathed in from God. They do not notice that the inbreathing of the divine Spirit is a kind of grace and advancement in dignity, so that man may be capable of the heavenly law.

The Lord shows in the gospel that the inbreathing was given to our father Adam, who already had a soul, and that it was not a soul breathed into him. For just as he had earlier breathed into Adam, so afterwards, after the resurrection, he himself breathed a greater grace of the divine Spirit into the apostles, who already had souls, saying: "Receive the Holy Spirit," and so on. He did not say, "Receive a soul," but, "Receive the Holy Spirit."

So the one who breathed into Adam, a man already made and having a soul, afterwards breathed into the blessed apostles, who had souls. This makes it known that all things were made through him and that without him nothing was made.

So there is no reason for anyone to suppose that the inbreathing is the soul. The soul is known to have been made, and it is placed under the conditions of the law and found liable to judgment. Of it he says: "Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Fear rather the one who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna."

So the inbreathing is not the soul but a grace of dignity. It comes from the divine Spirit, from God Christ, to all. Those who have it and keep it receive an increase of graces, like the apostles, the prophets and all the righteous.

But the unrighteous neglect and despise it, and so lose this great merit of dignity, like Saul, of whom it was said: "The Spirit of the Lord departed from him, and an unclean spirit troubled him." And scripture testifies that the spirit of wisdom will not enter a malicious soul.

Another heresy says that man's soul was not called a soul when God made it. Before, they say, it was called intellect and was in heaven. Afterwards, because it desired earthly things, it left heaven, and they think it was named soul for that reason. They do not know that in the beginning the soul was made and created by God after the angels, and was called soul by the Lord. It received this proper name from God, so that it was called soul and not intellect. As scripture says: "His soul will dwell among good things."
And again: "For you will not abandon my soul to hell." And again: "Return, my soul, to your rest." And again: "My soul is greatly troubled."

And again: "So my soul longs for you, O God." And again: "Blessed be the Lord, who made my soul." That view, then, belongs to the empty opinions of the philosophers. Divine scripture does not teach it.

There is another heresy which holds that cattle, serpents and birds are rational, like human beings. This is what the Manichees and the lost Gnostics suppose, along with some of the most foolish of the poets and the Stoic philosophers. They do not know that a rational human being has the understanding of the soul concerning God, that is, the ability to know about God and to believe, but has bodily sense in common with cattle and all the other creatures like them.

These can indeed have bodily sense, but they can in no way have the soul's understanding concerning God, nor an immortal and rational soul as a human being has. For a human being has been called the image of God, as Scripture says:
“Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding.” And: “Man, when he was held in honour, did not understand; he was compared to senseless cattle and became like them.”

So the sense of cattle, birds and serpents is shared with us through the body, but understanding belongs to human beings alone. It is a power of the immortal soul, poured into it by the Holy Spirit, and that soul has been called the image of God. It rules over all these creatures, governs them and possesses everything in abundance, as it is written: “I have given all things into your power.”

There is another heresy which says that wicked kings and false prophets do not come and arise by their own will, but are sent in by God's command. Its followers do not know that the Scriptures do not proclaim that such men become false prophets or wicked kings by God's doing. On the contrary, the Scriptures declare that they arise in this way against God's will, by their own will and at the prompting of the enemy,

just as Jannes and Jambres came of their own will, under Pharaoh, against blessed Moses and Aaron, the priests of God. For Scripture says: “They have reigned, but not through me, nor through my Spirit, says the Lord.” And about false prophets it says this: “Thus says the Lord to the false prophets: I did not send them, yet they went out to prophesy in my name.”

For this reason the Lord often pronounces against them a fitting sentence of death even in this world. So false prophets are not sent by God, nor are impious kings who turn away [?] from the Lord. And if at times, with the Lord's permission, the wicked are stirred up against the wicked, this happens so that the wicked may be destroyed by the wicked.

For the good, when they endure persecution and have righteousness before the Lord, await the great promise of a reward to come. The wicked, on the other hand, are sometimes put to death by the wicked and not only by the good, so that their iniquity may be partly punished even in this age.

There is another heresy which thinks that earthquakes happen not by God's command and anger but from the very nature of the elements. It does not know what Scripture says: “He looks upon the earth and shakes it with an earthquake.” And again: “I will shake heaven and earth.”

Paying no attention to God's power, these people dare to ascribe this movement to the power of the elements' nature, like certain empty-talking philosophers who attributed it to the nature of things and did not recognize God's power.

For in things of this kind too God's anger and power are at work, and he shakes his own creation for the sake of conversion, and indeed for the benefit of the many who sin and then return to the Lord, their Saviour and Creator.

There is another heresy which, following the vanity of the pagans, professes various names for the stars. So did the famous Hermes Trismegistus, who should be judged empty rather than great, and certain poets very like him, who in their raving assert names such as comets, “bearded stars,” the Hyades, the Kids and others of this kind. Yet Scripture declared to us a few names of the stars through the blessed prophet Job, before the pagans had taken the names of the stars over from the holy Scriptures.

For Job himself says: “He who made the Pleiades and Arcturus and Hesperus and the treasuries of the south and Orion and Lucifer.” These names alone, then, we receive as announced in the holy Scriptures. Scripture did not tell the names of all the stars, but reserved them to the power of God, declaring through the prophet: “He counts the multitude of the stars and calls them all by name.”

So the poets and false philosophers, reading these few names in the holy Scriptures, afterward dared to appropriate them for their own lies, to add many others, and to proclaim seeds of impiety to the world. They imagined that from these they could hope to grasp the names of all the stars, or of most of them. Yet no one but God Christ, through whom the Father made all things, has set and known the names of all the stars and called each of them by its own name, as it is written.

There is another heresy which is in doubt about language and languages, since Scripture speaks both of one language and of languages. If, then, there was one language at first because people were few, and afterward many because people born into the world had already multiplied, it is not so unprofitable to understand the matter in this way.

For after the fifteenth generation, from Adam to holy Eber, there were two thousand seven hundred years. In Eber's time the confusion of languages was sent, because of the sin they had committed in building the tower and the city, and they suffered this as rebels against God.

For they had an angelic grace, that is, knowledge of many languages, but they did not acknowledge the Lord as the giver of such great wisdom. By trying to advance against him they lost the grace which had been granted to them by God without any toil, a gift the Lord had given beforehand, without study and by nature, to all, as to the image of God.

Afterward, however, when the Lord had sent forgetfulness upon them, they could scarcely learn by study and teaching. Not all of them could, and not many languages but barely a few, so that someone might manage to learn three or four, and even then could hardly speak them.

Nevertheless, all the knowledge of languages that people had lost through their offence two thousand seven hundred years before, the Lord, after his ascension, again bestowed on believers under the blessed apostles through the Holy Spirit, without any toil, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles.

For to know the languages of all people belongs to angelic power, but through faith in Christ the knowledge of all languages is supplied to believers without toil. So we read that, as the divine Spirit taught them, the apostles, and likewise the Gentiles who at that time believed in Christ the Lord and Saviour, proclaimed the knowledge of all languages given them without toil,

as happened under Peter and Paul and others. When they taught the Gentiles, the Spirit of God came from God, and the Gentiles were able to speak in many languages. The people who heard marvelled at the Gentiles, that they too, through faith in Christ, had been granted knowledge of so many languages without instruction.

There is another heresy which says that the name of language came first from the Jews, while others say from the pagans. Both, in thinking this, have been deceived by no small error. For man, when he was made, shared in reason: [?] How, then, could one who spoke by reason be a stranger to reason?

So it comes first to share in reason and to be called rational, before having a particular, local name for some language and possessing anything from the name of a people. For two thousand seven hundred years had passed from Adam to Eber.

So the name of the language of all people was one, and the language was one. But once they plotted against God, that heavenly knowledge was taken from them, that is, the understanding and wisdom of all languages. Holy Eber, however, did not depart from God, in keeping with his name. So God willed that his race should spread more widely and should be the first in the world to be called by this name, so that from Eber, who had not consented to the building of the rebels' tower, they would be called Hebrews.

Eber, then, a most righteous man, is known to have lived before not only the pagans but also the Jews, that is, seven hundred years earlier. Because he believed in God and kept apart from the conspiracy of wicked men, he was found worthy to obtain from the Lord this first naming after his own name.

This is also why the empty poets, transferring that building to their own lies, taught that giants, the rebellious Aloadae, sought to climb up to heaven by piling mountains one on another, and that they were condemned for it. Their ravings have no longer been hidden from Christian knowledge and learning.

There is another heresy which is in doubt about the year announced by the prophet Isaiah when he says: “To proclaim the acceptable year of God and the day of recompense.” Some think that from the Lord's coming to the end of the world the number of years will be neither more nor less than three hundred and sixty-five, until the divine presence of Christ the Lord comes again from heaven. Anyone who thinks so is found to be contradicted by the facts.
For we know that four hundred years and more have already passed and been completed since the Lord came. How, then, can this account of the year hold, as a great many have chosen to think?

For the Lord ordered that only what he did and taught in a single year should be written down, not what he had done and said earlier in his first thirty years. So says blessed John, who says that the world could not contain the books if everything he had done were written.

So the prophet Isaiah was speaking of that year of the Lord and Saviour in which he taught, up to his passion, resurrection and ascension into heaven, as the most blessed apostles have also handed down. He was not speaking of three hundred and sixty-five years, as some suppose, but of that year after his baptism, in which, preaching to believers, he opened up the mysteries of salvation, bearing witness to and fulfilling what had been spoken long ago in the law and the prophets alike.

There is another heresy which asserts that the end of the world has not been fixed by God Christ the Saviour according to a determined measure of times. From this they suppose that the number of the end is certain [?], and they think it is neither more nor less. Yet the prophets have declared on every side that the end of the world will come around the five hundredth year, and that the Lord will then come again from heaven.

For Daniel counts seventy weeks, having heard from Christ the Lord: “Hear, man of desires: seventy weeks have been decreed for your people until Christ the prince, so that everything that has been foretold concerning the city of Jerusalem and the people may come to pass.”

This was told to Daniel before Christ came in the flesh, and it was almost completed then. In the same way the same number also holds after the Lord's incarnation [?]. Up to the law that Moses received and up to the entry into the promised land, you will find a number not very far from five hundred years.
So when the Lord spoke of various signs that would come near the end, famines, persecutions, floods, earthquakes and plagues, he also spoke to blessed Peter in a riddle about the number of years.
When Peter said, “Lord, how often shall I forgive my brother when he sins?” the Lord said, “Not seven times, but seventy

times seven.” By this he showed that a person must forgive another an unlimited number of the daily sins of the human race, whether the one returning is a Jew or a pagan. All others too, carnal people who return from impiety to the faith of Christ and to his catholic Church, must have every debt forgiven them once they believe.

For the Jewish historians too taught that four hundred and eighty years and more passed after Daniel, and that the Lord then came in the flesh. You also have a mystery most plainly announced in Genesis: vengeance sevenfold for Cain, but seventy times sevenfold for Lamech. There is no doubt that by this Scripture foretold without hesitation [?] the impiety of one people and the iniquity of the other, in two persons.

For the law is spiritual, according to the apostle, and “these,” he says, “are two covenants.” We do not set aside the history, that the people spent seventy years in Persia, nor do we despise the spiritual meaning. So the seventy weeks spoken of by Daniel, four hundred and ninety years, were then almost completed, and so Christ came in the flesh. And from the presence of Christ to the end of the world you will find that almost the same number of years is to be completed.

For those first wise interpreters taught that the seventy weeks Daniel saw are seven times seventy, that is, four hundred and ninety years [?]. This was the jubilee in the law, which the Jews, not those of today but the learned ones of old, that is, [?] the year of Christ's remission and forgiveness, [?] celebrating his bodily presence beforehand in figure, awaited with the greatest joy, as is contained in Leviticus. For the lesser jubilee has fifty years, no fewer [?],

and it cannot have more. For the greater jubilee has five hundred years [?], the lesser jubilee fifty. So the greater has five hundred years less ten, so that by this one jubilee might declare the presence of Christ and the end of the world.

The seventy years of the people's captivity in Persia are taken historically, and from their return to Jerusalem to the incarnation of Christ the Lord almost five hundred years are found to have been completed. Yet this must also be understood spiritually: after seventy times seven, that is, after about four hundred and ninety years, the Jews must [?] under the Antichrist, when he has been found to be a deceiver by the very Jews who had at first thought him to be the Christ.

Not long afterward, when his treachery and deceit have become known, those who remain will repent and all flock to the faith of Christ the Lord. Repenting of their sins, they will obtain pardon from Christ the Lord himself, as the rest have, so that what was said may be fulfilled:

“Truly I tell you, you will not see me again until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord’”; and so that this may be fulfilled: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in, and so all Israel will be saved,” as it is written; and: “Though the people of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved.”

Blessed Isaiah plainly taught about Christ that he would forgive all who return, and the Lord himself said this: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense.”

About this, when the Lord had taken the book in the temple and looked through this passage, he told the apostles and everyone that it had now been fulfilled in his presence. The most blessed Daniel also paid attention to this, when the Lord had said to him: “Hear, man of desires, and take note from the going forth of the word of God,” that is, from the incarnation of Christ, and from his divine presence coming again from heaven and the end of the world, which will take place with the angels.

There is another heresy which asserts about the giants that angels mingled with women before the flood, and they suppose that the giants were born from this. Yet Nimrod was born later, not from a spirit, that is, not from an angel, but from a man, Cush, who was the son of Ham. He is the first to be called a giant in Scripture, because he began to be a hunter and a mighty man, so that he was called a giant on the earth. Hence, it says, people would say, “Like Nimrod the giant, so mighty is he,” if anyone was later seen to be like him in strength.

So they were men who were strong and from their youth rapacious, ravagers, spear-throwers, runners, devoted to plunder. They were therefore regarded as strangers not only to the ways of human beings but even to their appearance, as monstrous; so that [?], committing such crimes contrary to the nature of other people, they were also called giants.

For by etymology “giant” means “earth-monster,” a word made of two names, whether because of form, way of life, appearance, strength or bulk of limbs. To show you that the giants were not of another nature but born of human stock, you also have the “six-fingered” men in the books of Kingdoms. The books of Kingdoms declared them to be of the race of giants, great in form, massive in limbs and of enormous strength, two thousand three hundred years after the flood,

like the famous Goliath, whom the most blessed David, king and prophet, struck down single-handed in battle. Of him and others like him it says: “[?] Carts carried their array of weapons.” So because men of this kind were given over to plunder from childhood in the manner of beasts, Scripture declared them to be strangers, as it were, to human nature and human ways.

For there is no doubt that the angels who were cast down from heaven are not like human nature. They were able only to suggest abominable things, contrary and against the law, as they also do to people now, entering into people, that is, persuading them;

just as the enemy of the human race persuaded the Jews to commit such crimes against the Lord and against the holy prophets, as it is written: “Satan entered into Judas.” So in the same way, in earlier times too, unclean spirits entered the souls of men and women and spread the crimes of evil persuasion throughout the world.

But if anyone thinks it right to hold that the angels sinned by being transformed into flesh, or believes that they remained in that flesh or were thus made fleshly, he forces the history by a violent reasoning. It is like the lies of the pagans and the poets, which claim that gods and goddesses were transformed and committed abominable unions.

If this had ever been done, there would be no doubt that it is done now as well. But what was never done has not been shown to happen now either. “Giant,” however, is also taken in a good sense, because of strength: “He will rejoice like a giant to run his course.” This is shown to have been proved and fulfilled in the divine presence of Christ.

There is another heresy which says that paganism was established by God, and was not devised by the malice of human beings and the prompting of the enemy for the sake of producing vices and crimes. If it was established by God, how is it condemned by the same God? For there is no doubt that knowledge of God the almighty Father, of his Son and of the Holy Spirit was proclaimed from the beginning of the world.

For you have it written in the book of the creation of the world, that is, in Genesis: “And God said, and God made”; and again: “God said: Let there be lights” [?]; and on the sixth day God said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.”

And it has been made plain that in creating man God acted, certainly not at an angel's persuasion, but with his Son, Christ our Lord, and the Holy Spirit. For you have the holy and adorable Trinity proclaimed to people of old in Genesis, that is, in the first book. For it says: “And the Lord rained sulphur and fire from the Lord.”

And again, concerning the Spirit on the first day: “And the Spirit of God was moving over the water.” And Pharaoh, king of Egypt, says: “Who will interpret these things for us, except one who has the Spirit of God?” And David: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the Spirit of his mouth.”

But afterward the depraved will of human beings, withdrawing from such great knowledge of godliness, hurried eagerly to serve the lies and vanities of idols and preferred to give itself to a most shameful life. So it was held liable to the judgment of condemnation, so that the prophets said beforehand: “Whoever sacrifices to gods will be rooted out.” And again: “The gods who did not make heaven will be rooted out.”

And so the Lord too was not showing a presence of his that was new, when he said: “I who spoke in the prophets, here I am.” Nowhere, then, has the Lord commanded that angels be worshipped, nor the elements of the world, nor any creature, nor idols. These the most wicked will of human beings chose to invent in order to commit its crimes and shameful deeds, so that by worshipping them people could have unbounded licence to do evil.

For the very name “idol” has been given, by Greek interpretation, as meaning “a semblance of deceit” and “a perversion of form.” So the Trinity of Christianity was preached from the beginning of the world, and the truth of godliness was taught everywhere without interruption. For David too says: “The Lord said to my Lord”; and: “Your good Spirit will lead me on the right way”; and again: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world”; and: “Where shall I flee from your Spirit, and where shall I go from your face?”

For blessed Solomon teaches that idolatry was established by a man who, once long mourning as a father for the son he had lost, made an image of him and took delight in looking at it. From him it was handed down to later generations, and from there all sorts of material for impiety sprang up among the human race.

There is another heresy which says that Christians were created more recently than the Jews and pagans, and after them. Its followers do not know that Christians were created before the Jews and pagans, by nature and by faith, in life and in time, in sacrifice and in their way of living.

In faith, certainly: for from Adam to Moses, over three thousand seven hundred years, all the righteous worshipped God and God, Lord and Lord, and also the Holy Spirit, and proclaimed the true Trinity. So you can learn the whole Trinity without effort from those blessed ones of former and ancient times [?], and see that this was afterwards made manifest to us as well by the Lord. For when Scripture says:

"The Lord rained sulphur and fire upon Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord," what does it seem to proclaim there? Did it not declare that God the Father accomplished all signs and wonders through his Son, that is, through Christ who is God? David knew this. When he proclaimed the Lord the Father and the Lord Christ, that is, his Word, together with the Holy Spirit, he proclaimed a Trinity of persons, yet of one majesty and substance, and of equal power in divinity.

Yet he showed explicitly that the Son is from God the Father, who is first [?], and likewise the Holy Spirit, when he taught: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power"; and again elsewhere: "The Lord said to my Lord." And all the prophets made proclamation about the Word and the Spirit, saying everywhere: "And the word of the Lord came to me," and: "The Spirit of the Lord," one says, "was upon me."

So Christianity is not something temporal with respect to faith. Before there were Jews and pagans, it had been made manifest in the law to those who studied and sought. But to those who did not grasp it, the knowledge of the almighty Father was scarcely proclaimed by those holy and perfect teachers.
In their life, too, those earlier saints followed no other way than the one in which we live.

For down to the most blessed Abraham they pleased God without having circumcision and without delighting in sacrifices, and he declared them righteous in all things. For David said: "The sacrifice for God is a contrite heart"; and: "Offer to God a sacrifice of praise." And the sacrifices imposed on the Jews under the pressure of necessity [?] were temporary, not perpetual or true, nor did they bring salvation. That is why the prophet says to the Jews: "Behold, I make new things," and: "Before they come, they have been announced to you."

So the prophet Isaiah testified to the Jews beforehand: "Who required these things from your hands?" And again: "Circumcise your hearts, and not your bodies." And what kind of sacrifice Melchizedek first offered in Abraham's time, four hundred and thirty years before the [?] Jews were named or Judah was born, and before they received [?], you may see in the book of Genesis. That sacrifice is the mystery of Christianity, so that you may recognize that everything in Christianity, whether faith or life or sacrament, is not temporal, but was established and proclaimed from the origin of the world, and indeed celebrated.

But in Christ and through Christ, through whom all things were made, it was fitting for us to see and know [?] from him, and to receive from him more fully, fulfilled and completed, that greater mystery in the law which had been proclaimed about him beforehand.

For there is no doubt that a similar chastity was found in a great many prophets: in blessed Elijah, holy Elisha, Daniel, Jeremiah, Ezra and the three youths, and many other most blessed men. Thus, when Christ was present, people would recognize that what was above the law had been proclaimed beforehand by them; marriage, which existed by the law, would be confirmed by his divine sentence; and this grace would be known to be left to the will and zeal of each person.

Therefore the Lord himself joined to us those earlier saints who lived before the law, and joined us to them, according to the faith of righteousness. But he rejected the Jews and pagans, who were placed in the middle period between the commandment and grace. Ruined by a hostile and destructive will, they are found in vices of the flesh. They are enemies and adversaries of the heavenly teaching, reserved for the eternal judgment of punishment.

There is another heresy which says that we are born pagans by nature, not Christians. That is, its followers suppose that a person's body and soul are not created daily by God through Christ in the natural order, but come into being through pagan vanity. Yet from Adam to Abraham, and afterwards down to Judah, who is the fourth generation after Abraham, people were not pagans, nor were they called Jews. They were called nations, named after their various provinces.

The name "pagans" came after the Jews. It comes either from pagus, that is, a place, or a single province, or from King Paganus, and the last has been shown to be true, as the Greek poet Hesiod says. If it comes from pagus, it points to a place, just as people still say today "from that pagus." But if it comes from idols, [?] because those who worshipped carved images were called pagans, that is, gentiles.

These idols were not invented by God but by the utterly depraved will of human beings. Both our Scripture and a great many pagan writings have declared that men invented them to seduce and damn souls, because the people who looked upon them took delight in feasts, and through the vanity of these things brought destruction on their souls.

But there is a sure and stronger proof: the pagans themselves record in their histories that they were named after King Paganus, as the Greek poet Hesiod says. Ever since King Paganus, son of Deucalion and Pyrrha, they have held his name as though it were praiseworthy and beloved, or rather they have honoured his memory down to the present day, and they still keep and cherish this lie of a name.

So Hellen, that is, a Greek, is named from the language and from the name of the king who was the son of Deucalion and bore that name. In the same way the Italians took their name from Italus, the Romans from Romulus and the Latins from Latinus, and not from the impiety of idols.

For idols, that is, the forms of carved images, were invented later by the utterly wicked will of men. The Greek language, on the other hand, marked out what was peculiar to a single province, and the pagan king confirmed it with his own name, just as Romulus named the Romans. As Hesiod says, the Greeks were named after a Greek king called Graecus, who was the son of Deucalion.

There is another heresy which says that the number of years since the origin of the world is uncertain and that people do not know the course of the ages. Yet from Adam to the flood there are ten generations and two thousand two hundred and forty-two years. From the flood to the confusion of tongues under holy Eber, who had not consented to the building of the tower, is the fifth generation, nearly six hundred years. At that time the names of the provinces were also divided, into some seventy-five languages. And from then to the blessed patriarch Abraham is the fifth generation, five hundred and forty years.

From Abraham to Moses there are seven generations, four hundred and thirty years, as the blessed apostle says. From Moses to Samuel the judge there are six hundred and twenty-nine years. From Samuel and David to the captivity of the Jews in Persia there are nearly five hundred years. From the captivity to the coming of our Lord there are nearly five hundred years. And from the Lord until now there are about four hundred and thirty years, more or less.

So if the faith that is in us was also in those earlier holy men, our fathers, and was handed down and preached by them before us (that is, this divine knowledge of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit), how is it temporal, as some suppose? And how could anyone say that this Christian knowledge was not proclaimed to all people from the origin of the world, when it is shown to have been revealed and preached in the commandment and the law?

If, in the middle period under Moses, something was said less fully and through a shadow, this was certainly not because the Lord who gave it begrudged it. Rather, the blame will fall on the people, who could not grasp the heavenly mystery, and on the weakness and frailty of human beings who lacked the strength.

Finally, Christ the Lord himself confirmed by his command what he had proclaimed earlier through the holy prophets, saying: "Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." He did this not only to declare that this faith is the ancient one, existing from the origin of the world, but also to prove that the life we live today lies in circumcision of the heart, not in boasting of the flesh.

So they are badly mistaken who dare to attribute the birth of human beings either to pagan impiety or to Jewish vanity. For no one may be called a Jew unless he has received [?] on the eighth day, and likewise no one may be called a pagan unless he has come to believe that vain gods made man.

Therefore the natural order is to be attributed to God, not to the vanity of either of these. But teaching, which comes after nature, if it is true, must be joined to faith in God and united to his most wholesome service. It does not depart from that service, but rather recognizes its Lord through faith and remembers its Creator by nature.

So what is to blame is not a weakness in the natural human mind but rather a depraved will, as the Lord says: "And now, if you are willing and listen to me, you will eat the good things of the land; but if you are unwilling and do not listen to me, the sword will devour you. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken this." And the Lord says: "Come to me, all you who are burdened, and I will lift you up."

There is another heresy which says that the names of the days (of the Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus and Saturn) were established by God in this form from the origin of the world, and were not given by the vain presumption of men. Yet from the first origin [?] down to the Greek kings and that utterly deceitful Hermes, who dared to give these utterly vain and frivolous names by lying, if you are willing to look into it,

you will find that a great deal of time passed, and that it was the pagans, that is, the Greeks, who gave these names, since [?] they also said, according to these names of the seven stars, that human birth is determined by them, as that raving man himself defines it. For the days were named by God by number, first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh. They were not announced or handed down at the beginning under these vain and utterly shameful names.

There is another heresy which says, following the empty opinion of certain philosophers, that there are infinite and innumerable worlds. Yet Scripture has spoken of one world and has taught us about one. These people take their ideas even from the apocryphal, that is, secret, writings of the prophets, as the pagans themselves have said,
like that Democritus who asserted that there are many worlds. By preaching this out of his own wisdom, he stirred up the souls and wavering minds of many to various errors.

There is a heresy which reads in Genesis the word of the Lord about Adam: "Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil; and now, lest he ever stretch out his hand and touch and taste of the tree of life and live forever," and then says that the Lord drove him out of paradise out of envy.

First of all, they believe that one god made the soul and another the flesh, as the Manichaeans, the Gnostics, the Nicolaitans and other lost souls suppose. They say that one god is good and the other, they claim, is evil in this world.

And they suppose that it was this evil god who ordered him to be driven out of paradise. They do not consider that one and the same God the Father made Adam our father through the Son, and gave him a commandment, so that by keeping it he might remain immortal, and that when the commandment was broken he was driven out of paradise, as it is written;
and that he suffered this through the persuasion of the enemy. Because they pay no heed to Christ's mercy, they go down into the abyss of eternal death.

So God did not drive our father out of paradise out of envy, to keep him from staying there or tasting of the tree of life. Rather, he did it for Adam's own good: he did not spare him when he sinned in a small matter, so that sparing him would not lead him, as he grew older, on to other and greater crimes, which God would then have to condemn more harshly once Adam had become guilty in a criminal judgment.

For between man and the devil, Christ was both hearer and most just judge, and good in all things. In the same way he did not spare the man who sinned in a small matter, but gave him too a fitting sentence for the sin he had committed, while likewise leaving the devil room for repentance.

But since the devil did not understand that he should repent of having suggested so great an evil, a greater judgment was kept for him afterwards. The man, when he was driven out of paradise, was found readier to repent; but the devil, since he is seen to be harder toward repentance, awaits a greater severity in the future judgment from Christ the Lord, as it is said: "He did not wish to understand, so as to do good."

And again: "But he did not hate wickedness." So because Adam, sinning in a small matter, received [?] when he had been persuaded by the devil to eat, and at once repented, he earned pardon for his offence, and a return to paradise in the presence of Christ, through the begetting of children as well.

But the devil, who did not repent, and his followers are reserved for a greater judgment, as the Lord said: "Depart from me [?] into the eternal fire, which my Father has prepared for the devil and his angels."

There are some heretics who think that our father Adam and our mother Eve were blind before they tasted of the tree, and that afterwards they opened their eyes and only then saw that they were naked. Yet Scripture has already said that Eve saw the tree and its fruit with her own eyes, that it was good to look at and pleasant to see, and that she stretched out her hand and tasted.

To think this way, then, belongs to the madness of heretics, or rather to the blindness of the Jews, since they do not understand what kind of nakedness [?]. Scripture taught us that this nakedness was the loss of immortality through the breaking of the commandment, not the nakedness of the body.

The apostle taught us this when he said: "If indeed, having put on Christ, we may not be found naked"; and again: "Put on Christ Jesus." And the Lord in the gospel [?] rebukes it, speaking to the man who had been invited to the wedding but had no wedding garment.

There is a heresy which hears in Genesis that after the transgression the Lord clothed our parents in tunics of skin, and supposes that he made their bodies at that moment and clothed them in this way. Yet Scripture had already said that on the seventh day God took earth from the clay and formed their bodies, and then afterwards made the woman's flesh from Adam's rib.

So here it was not calling their bodies tunics of skin. Rather, it was declaring that by divine power he gave them the wisdom to make clothing for their bodies, as it is written: "Who gave women wisdom for making garments?"

But if anyone wants to take it that the Lord made tunics for them, [?] the Almighty made it from nothing, as it is written: "He who calls into being from nothing the things that are not, as though they were."
So if they made the tunics by their own wisdom, as the prophet says, that is reasonable; and if God provided this for them by his own power, that is not unfounded either.
For in the temple women and virgins worked purple, fine linen, flax and other materials for the honour and covering of the temple, and also various and diverse adornments for the temple.

There is a heresy which reads in Exodus that an angel met Moses at the lodging where they had stopped and wanted to kill him, rather than his son who had not yet been circumcised, and takes no small offence at this.

If someone wishes to understand it in this way, that the angel was threatening him because the appointed days, that is, eight, had passed (on the eighth day a male child had to be circumcised), and they had not done it and had thus despised God's command [?]. And so the fault of children of tender age is not theirs so much as their parents', as it is written.

So, understanding that the fault was the parents' and not the infant's, "At once," it says, "his mother took a stone and circumcised the boy." When the angel saw the blood, he immediately withdrew from him and entirely removed the penalty of death he had been threatening to inflict.

For Moses is not found to have been circumcised at that hour, as some suppose; it was his son who was circumcised. What had been commanded earlier, under the patriarchs and the law, was carried out by the people, or by the parents of some, slowly and not promptly, as it is written.

There are some heretics who are troubled about Deuteronomy. When Moses was about to depart from the body, he composed this book by repeating material from the four books, and in it he lays down, as it were, the foundations of the earlier law. Because it bears greater witness to Christ's bodily coming, these people fall into no small error and think otherwise. For what was written earlier in the law, that is, in Exodus, is contained in this same book as well:

only this seems to have been said by him in addition, since he added: "The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among our brothers; you shall listen to him as you listen to me. And if anyone does not listen to him, he will be rooted out entirely."

For some think it is called Deuteronomy because in it he received once again on the mountain the inscribed tablets of stone. But in Exodus he is known to have received them twice and to have gone up the mountain twice.

It is reasonable, then, that what belonged to the law and to grace should be revealed concerning Christ the Lord: that what was celebrated in the law through a shadow should be proclaimed, among believers, as heavenly grace poured out in Christ's bodily presence, and that it should be written down in this very book and handed on to all as a testimony.

There are some heretics who hear that blessed David said in the fiftieth psalm, "I was conceived in iniquity, and in sin my mother bore me," and suppose that the prophet said this because he considered the lawful right of marriage to be iniquity and sin. Yet God had already said in the book of Genesis: "Be born and multiply, and fill the earth"; and Scripture says: "Marriage is to be honoured," and so on.

For if anyone thinks this way, then so many great righteous men were conceived in iniquity, even though they were sanctified in the womb, such as the patriarchs, the prophets, the judges, blessed Jeremiah and most blessed John the Baptist, as it is written.

But they do not know that the blessed prophet David spoke in another sense. He was not speaking of natural birth but of the transgression of Adam our father and of Eve, who were driven out of paradise after breaking the commandment and then had children. He was teaching that Eve, the mother of all as it were, conceived and gave birth in this way after the iniquity of breaking the commandment.

For how could David say of himself that he was conceived in iniquity and born in sin, when he was born in lawful wedlock and was chosen by God and sought out for such great royal glory, as is written of him?

So here he was not teaching that he himself had been conceived in iniquity or born in sin. He wanted to point to our parents Adam and Eve: having first committed sin, that is, the breaking of the commandment, they afterwards had children, and from them all of us are likewise brought to birth.

That is why, after the transgression, Scripture says: "In pain you shall bring forth children." For we have from those first parents the iniquity of transgression, common to all flesh and universal, passed down to everyone from that first inheritance, as the apostle said: "Just as through one man death entered into all men."

For this right of marriage, established by God, is praised daily and customarily blessed. He showed that what came first was sorrow, and he announced that the heavenly grace of Christ would bring great joy to believers, saying: "Unless someone is reborn of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven."

That is why, in that psalm, foreseeing the joy to come, he testified: "You will sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow," so that through him we too, believing, may rejoice together with him in saving baptism.

There are certain heretics who do not think rightly about the division of the world and the apportioning of its inhabited lands. They argue that it was the Greeks, the Egyptians or the Persians who first began to describe the whole world, and not blessed Noah who, after the flood, divided it among his three sons, gave it to them, set its bounds and apportioned it in order.

Later historians took this up as if following certain paths, and made up various falsehoods. Blessed Noah, then, divided the whole world among his three sons, Shem, Ham and Japheth. To Shem he gave the eastern regions of India and of the Persians, extending into some part of the south, the west and the north, as far as Mount Lebanon, and by a fixed decree he confirmed that his firstborn would have his borders there.

To Ham, his second son, he allotted by decree all the Syrias, the diocese of Egypt, Africa, and the vast breadth of Ethiopia stretching toward the borders of the ocean and of the Spains. Through the divine Spirit he foretold that Ham would possess and inhabit these lands, and in the middle he granted him borders reaching as far as Cappadocia, that is, the Taurus range.

To the third, named Japheth, he assigned by divine command the cold regions that lie as one enters Cappadocia and leaves Cilicia, namely those of Armenia, the Bosporus, Pontus, Thrace, the Pannonias, Illyricum and Italy, together with all the parts of the west. From the first son, Scripture counts twenty-five generations as descended; from the second, thirty-five,

that is, from Ham. But to Japheth, for whom a smaller number of generations was reckoned at that time, only fifteen, blessed Noah promised that a larger and more desirable posterity would come in the future, as Scripture says: "May the Lord enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem."

So although only a small number of generations was found to have been granted to this youngest son at that time, his number was later to grow and increase beyond that of his two brothers, so that he would hold the empires both of the middle and of the farthest regions, that is, of the Canaanites, Egyptians, Africans and Persians.

From him the Romans were later born, conquerors of the world and rulers of all nations. From this we know that the Romans, Latins and Italians trace their descent from Japheth, and that they hold the world under their sway every day, as they often did before.

Whatever the falsehood of the Greeks would have us think ancient is proven in every way to be recent, as their own authors testify. Solon told the Athenians what he had heard from an Egyptian priest, who said to him:

"Solon, Solon, you Greeks are always new, always children. No Greek will ever be old or ancient, and you have no ancient teaching or knowledge; what you have you have snatched and seized from others, and you set it out altered by various lies, and in that form you teach people." So Plato says in the Timaeus.

For after the confusion of tongues, various names began to spring up. Two or three Greek historians took these and wrote various records, as it were, and when they wished to cloud over and conceal how recent they were, they were judged and proven by their own witnesses to be the greatest of liars.

For when fifty of them, Greeks, Egyptians, Chaldeans and Syrians, agree about our antiquity, and two or three disagree, it is right to accept the many historians who speak with one voice rather than the two or three who are out of tune, because the many have spoken the truth rather than the two.

There is another heresy which says that the flood in the time of Deucalion and Pyrrha was more ancient than the one that took place under blessed Noah. The pagans borrowed this story, changed the names, and claim in the same way that there was an ark in Greece after the flood. And what is recent, belonging to the most empty paganism, is proclaimed by them as though it were

ancient, with much falsehood; and what happened in Thessaly, in a small area, is taught by the thieving pagans as if it had happened everywhere, that is, in the whole world. Such floods do occur in Thessaly from time to time, sometimes in quite a small area, but that flood happened over the whole world, as even the writings of the gentiles themselves bear witness.

There is another heresy which says that people are born according to the twelve signs of the zodiac. So say those most empty astrologers, champions of every error and crime, and very many unlearned people who hear them sometimes abandon the law of God and do not hesitate to serve the vanities of the astrologers. In this the apostle's saying is fulfilled:

"They worshipped and served [?] the creature rather than the Creator." And again: "See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the elements of the world and not according to Christ; for in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily."

They do not know, then, that these twelve signs, as they call them, are different climates and different regions of the world, arranged by God to be inhabited, and that different temperaments of places and seasons were established, hot, cold, dry and moist, from the four corners of the world.

From these the winds pour forth like fountains full of their own quality, blowing upon one another with the great power proper to each, and a healthful mixture arises. Then, as this mixture spreads everywhere, a pleasant and wholesome temperateness is supplied from it to all who dwell there. Thus it is well known that a sweet and prosperous life is granted and bestowed on mortals by the Lord through divine power.

There is another heresy which says that the souls of poisoners, criminals, murderers and others like them pass into demons, cattle, beasts and serpents. They do not know that when a person's soul leaves this world, whether good or bad, that is, godly or ungodly, it is led by an angel to an appointed place, so that in the future it may receive according to what it did while it lived in this world.

If anyone supposes that it happens in the way they say, he seems to share in paganism and the vanity of the philosophers rather than in Christianity, since the apostle says: "We must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what he has done in this body." And again: "For you will not abandon my soul to hell." And again: "But in hell who will confess you?"

The nature of the soul, then, is not changed into another nature. But when by its own will it despises and neglects God's commandment, and declines to hold fast to lawful and saving pursuits, it devotes itself to punishment at the coming judgment, and is recognized as comparable to nothing but cattle in its conduct: not in nature, but in conduct, as it is written.

So people of this kind, pagans, Jews and very many others, become like cattle in this world not in nature but in conduct. For when the Savior said to the Jews, "You are of your father the devil," he meant it not by nature; he was accusing and judging them to be like him in wicked conduct and brutish thoughts. And John said to the Jews: "Brood of vipers." [?]

There are other heretics who say that the Lord descended into hell and there also proclaimed himself to all who had died, so that those who confessed him there would be saved. But this is contrary to what the prophet David says: "But in hell who will confess you?" And the apostle: "All who have sinned without the law will perish without the law."

When the Lord says, "It will be more tolerable for some than for that city which has not believed," meaning the teaching of the apostles and the gospel, he is comparing many punishments and saying that some endure lesser torments than others; he does not, however, affirm that they are saved on that account.

For whoever thinks that the false poets and vain philosophers, rebels against God, can be saved errs worse than they do and departs from the truth. It was none other than those vain poets and philosophers who sowed the seeds of pagan ungodliness, the names of gods and goddesses, in people's minds. Meanwhile the prophet cries out about the coming judgment, asking to be forgiven here through repentance, and says:

"Forgive me, that I may be refreshed, before I go and am no more." If, then, the righteous who sinned scarcely obtained pardon through repentance while still in this life [?], as Solomon says: "And if the righteous will scarcely be saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?" For if they had believed that God exists, they would not have sown the shameful names of gods and goddesses, and they would have obtained pardon when Christ descended into hell.

Since, then, the ungodly and the enemies of God are everywhere, how will they be saved by confessing there after death? The apostle teaches that every person must die and after this be judged, as it is written, before the judgment seat of Christ, and receive according to what he did in this world.

The Savior confirms this, saying of them that they did not believe even the Father; and so he declared that they too must be judged. But whoever believed in the Father before Christ came in the flesh has passed beyond the judgment of the ungodly.

When sinners and the ungodly are compared, there is a difference in punishments and blows. Neither is fully acquitted; rather, there is just judgment and a recompense fitting the sin, even for those who were swallowed up by the waters in Noah's time, as Scripture has taught.

There is another heresy which is uncertain about the origin of the soul and supposes that it is made up of the elements. So many most empty philosophers suspect that the human soul is now of fire, now of water, now of breath, now of matter, now of a spring, now of atoms, now something like air. But the soul was made by the Lord, out of nothing, as it is written: "Who made all things out of nothing, so that the things which were not might be."

So the soul, made by God, is called the image of God, and it was made after the creation of the angels; for man is lower than the nature of the angels, as it is written: "You made him a little lower than the angels."

But if he keeps the commandments of the law, then he will be like the angels. If, then, the angels, who are servants of God, are placed under law, how much more is the soul of man under the law, which has been proclaimed [?]. If it keeps what it has been commanded, then it ought to say what the Lord told the apostles: "And when you have done all things, say: We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were commanded."

There is another heresy which says of the Savior that he was first with the Father and was then born. When they confess it simply in this way, they give people various occasions of stumbling, for to exist beforehand and then afterwards to be born is in every way a contradiction.

His generation is indeed twofold: one belongs to his divinity, unbounded and eternal; the other to his taking flesh through the Virgin, in time; and of this there is no doubt. Yet according to his divinity we must recognize that he was never not with the Father, and that he who was always with the Father was not from himself, as though he were not known to be begotten of the Father, as some suppose in their error.

So both statements, if presented with sound interpretation, prove to be the foundation of right faith. We are to recognize him as truly begotten of the Father, this only Son; yet not in time. Rather, as is fitting, we are to recognize and believe that he was truly begotten of the Father before all ages and all creation, and we must not forget that he remains with the Father forever and has always remained.
There is therefore no separation or contradiction between always being, having been, and being begotten.

"Always being" is said because of his eternity, so that the Son may not be thought temporal; "begotten" is said because the Church, in its preaching, knows that he was born not from himself but from the Father.

So the one is not to be separated from the other. The Son's eternity and his generation must be joined and linked together, and our confession concerning the Father must be believed and held in such a way that we recognize one Father who begets and one only Son of the Father, truly begotten of the Father.

Therefore it is right for godly faith to confess both that he always is and that he is begotten, so that his eternal generation is not temporal, and the true distinctness and eternity of the only-begotten Son, from the Father and with the Father, is not forgotten. But if anyone confesses that he was first unbegotten and then afterwards begotten of the Father, he does not know what he is confessing.

For while he thinks he is escaping one heresy, he runs into another and worse one: by confessing the Son unbegotten, he in fact denies both Father and Son, proclaims two unbegotten beings, and denies the distinction between the one unbegotten Father and the one only-begotten Son, truly from the Father.

There are certain heretics who take in this way what the Lord said about Pharaoh through Moses: "For this purpose I have raised you up, to show my power in you"; and: "I will surely harden Pharaoh's heart, so that he will not let you go." And the apostle says: "So it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy."

But the apostle says these things not as a definition but as an argument, teaching what is true, so that no one should think that God spoke in that sense. For one must pay attention to what the Lord says: "That I may show in you all my power," that is, his magnanimity, goodness and forbearance, which are indeed poured out on all people in this world.

For when he speaks to Pharaoh, he speaks to every person living in the body, and he addresses them in their prosperity, in their wealth and temporal power. When people give their attention to riches, they become more sluggish and careless about the fear and grace of God and of Christ, and so they forget their own salvation at the end and lose all thought of the fear of God.
For when Pharaoh himself was afflicted, he acknowledged God against his will, as it is written; and when God again let him go, he returned like a dog to its vomit.

So the souls of all pagans, Jews, heretics and the rich, and of sinners alike, are sometimes found to despise God when they prosper. Therefore discipline is useful and salutary for the human race in all things, as the prophet says: "It is good for me, O Lord, that you humbled me, so that I might learn your statutes"; and again, concerning rebuke:

"When he slew them," he says, meaning the Lord slaying the Jews, "then they sought him and kept watch for him." So the blessed apostle does not say either "Let us not run" or "Let us not will to serve God." Rather, we must first run by our own will, and then not presume or boast that we deserve to be saved by our own strength and righteousness rather than by the mercy of Christ.

For whoever runs with pride and presumption does not hope for protection from God, since he presumes that his righteousness comes from his own way of life. So the blessed apostle teaches us both to run and to will, and that it lies in our will to persevere in humility in this very course of good works, and only then to hope that salvation may be obtained from the Lord himself, as the Lord says:

"And when you have done all things, say: We are most worthless servants." [?] "And if the righteous is scarcely saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?" So there are some things within us for which we must run. But there are greater things that must be hoped for and obtained from God, as the apostle says:

"You do not know what you are asking." Suppose, for example, someone says, "I can be a martyr," or "I can be an apostle," and does not say, "If God, Christ, wills." The increase of such a gift and grace is conferred by him, and is not acquired by the vain presumption and boasting of men. A will of this kind belongs to someone who is testing God and presuming, not to someone who seeks and implores that he may be found worthy to attain so great a dignity.

There are certain heretics, such as the Manichaeans, the Gnostics, the Nicolaitans and others, who dare to say of blessed David that he was not a prophet of Christ the Lord, nor a teacher and expounder of all the divine Scriptures, but that he was a writer of human songs and worldly matters. Yet he was found worthy, beyond many, to proclaim to the human race the mysteries of heavenly grace and the saving secret of Christ the Lord.

For just as Christ the Lord gave various graces to other saints, so to David he granted greater knowledge, as the Lord says: "I will give you," he says, "the sure holy things of David"; and: "I have found David son of Jesse, a man who will do all that is in my heart," says the Lord.

They do not know, then, that David, king and prophet, sent by the Lord, was a swift and most powerful expounder of the divine Scriptures. Through him all that had been said before, all that was seen in his own time, and all that was announced for the future was to be proclaimed to the human race, gathered together in brief. In three verses of the first psalm he set out the whole force of things, the truth of things past, present and to come, announcing all the errors and various crimes of every people, when he says:

"Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly," that is, of the pagans, "and has not stood in the way of sinners," that is, of the Jews, "and has not sat in the seat of pestilence," that is, of the heretics. And from here, as from fountains and abundant sources, he taught the various seeds of iniquity that would come upon the human race, so that these three evils, paganism, Judaism and every heresy, might be despised and condemned, and the one true faith alone, that of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, believed by all, might be practiced.

For blessed David, moved by divine zeal at that time, when he saw people sacrificing to demons and not to God, set up four choirs in the city of Jerusalem, facing the four quarters of the world, seventy-two in each. He also appointed four men from among the singers, and there were countless others besides, guarding the precinct of God on every side from without.

With these choirs placed around him, the most blessed patriarch David himself sang psalms with the people in the midst. As so great a witness of the incarnation of Christ the Lord, predestined by the Lord, he offered in song the various joys and praises of the psalms to none other than Christ the Lord himself. Three times every day, with the prayers of the psalms and with resounding song, he rejoiced together with all the people, proclaiming the divine presence of Christ and promising the world the joys that would come from it.

Of this the Lord deigned to say that many prophets and wise men had longed to see and hear what the apostles were privileged to hear and see. For it is plain to everyone from the chronology that even what passes for the wisdom of the Greeks comes from the law and the prophets, and especially from blessed David.

And so the poets and other wise men tried, in imitation of him, to fashion in verse what they wished to say. They took their themes from the law and the prophets, changed the names, and in their haste to violate the rights of truth they sowed in the world the various lies of their own faithlessness.

Hence very many worldly and unlearned people, knowing nothing of this, would rather cultivate and follow the recent lies of the pagans than the ancient and true mysteries and foundations of the saving Christian law.

From their own vanities, then, that is, from the Greek historians, anyone can learn how recent the empty wisdom of the Greeks is. And as their own people gradually come to recognize this, it is without doubt spurned, trampled underfoot and condemned every day.

There are other heretics who fall into no small error over the disordered arrangement of the Psalter, thinking that the whole book of Psalms is not by most blessed David. When they look for the history in sequence, they find it out of order: they see that what is last has been placed first and what is first has been placed last, and they are greatly scandalized.

For in the third psalm he suffers persecution from his son, while in a psalm past the hundredth he is described fighting against the foreigner; yet we find that he first fought Goliath in his youth, and only afterwards, in old age, endured war from his son.
And although these things are to be understood spiritually of Christ, those who diligently inquire into the history of this blessed prophet are nonetheless troubled by no small stumbling block.

Again, the book of Psalms says that the hymns of David ended after seventy-two psalms, yet afterwards his name is again announced in the titles of many psalms. They complain about this as well, asking why it was arranged so, not knowing that the various joys of the psalms were rightly bestowed by the Lord on the blessed king and prophet. So even if titles bearing the names of others are found in the psalms, nevertheless the sum of all this praise was afterwards granted by Christ to this author and founder, as prophet, king and patriarch.

As for the disordered arrangement of the psalms with respect to the history, the most diligent authors who have interpreted them said this: captivity often befell the Jewish people at the hands of the gentiles because of idolatry, since the Jews worshipped idols along with them [?]; and at such times the divine Scriptures were sought out and burned by the gentiles.

But if anyone had hidden some part of the psalms, then afterwards, when peace returned, these same divine Scriptures were sought out by a few holy men. When they were found, the wise men of that time received them, for there were no longer prophets, only priests; and, held back by fear, they arranged the text of the psalms just as they had received it from various people, and ordered it to be set out in that sequence.

If, then, there is disorder with respect to the history, as many have said, this seems to be the reason. But it is clear to the diligent that, within this very disorder of the psalms, a spiritual and consistent knowledge of Christ is to be recognized: what is said of Christ at the beginning is likewise said in the middle, and what was to come afterwards was said of him beforehand everywhere. That is why the apostle says: "Christ yesterday and today, the same," he says, "also for ever and ever."

For there is no doubt that the psalms were spoken by spiritual power, so as to show that what was done earlier through the devil in the ungodliness of idols was the same crime committed under the Jews by his seduction; and the catholic Church, in its preaching, knows well that the perversity of the heretics, springing up daily at the end of time, is his work as well.

There are heretics who misunderstand the passage in the book of Genesis where the Lord said to Cain: "You have sinned; be still. Its turning is toward you, and you shall rule over it." For when he says, "You shall rule over it," they think he was telling him: "You will be lord over your brother."

Someone might read it that way because Cain was older than his most blessed brother Abel, and under the law those older by birth were also greater in honor, that is, by right of the firstborn. Even so, "You shall rule over it" does not mean "You will be his lord." That reading is wrong in every respect.

For if that were so, how could the Lord pass sentence of death on him for having killed his brother, as it is written? So Scripture does not say here that he would rule over his brother and so kill him. It says: "You shall rule over your thought," your evil thought. This lies within your choice and within the will of every person. Each must either cast out of his heart the evil thought sent in by the devil, or, by not casting it out, incur everlasting guilt.

Christ the Lord searches the heart and mind of man, and he saw clearly what Cain was hiding. He rebuked him for what he had been planning and warned him not to commit that crime and so sow in the world the way of murder among kin.

This is also what is said in the Gospel: "If you have anger against your brother, go and be reconciled, and then afterward offer your gift." David likewise says: "Be angry, and do not sin." And he goes on to explain what "Be angry, and do not sin" means: "What you say in your hearts, repent of upon your beds."

Solomon also says: "If the spirit of the enemy who rules rises up against you, give him no place to dwell in you." And the Lord says: "Whoever is angry with his brother without cause will be liable to judgment." So the Lord taught that the thought and suggestion of the enemy must be driven out at once. If it stays long in a person, it makes him more inclined and provokes him to commit the crime.

There is a heresy that does not rightly understand the passage about Cain. It holds that after the fratricide he had committed, he asked the Lord to let him die rather than be let go, saying: "The cause is greater [?] if I am let go," and: "It will be that everyone who finds me will kill me."

But through that one man the Lord was teaching a general pattern for the whole human race. Through repentance he was granting the abundant pardon of his goodness, so that once the crime had ceased, the fruit of good works would follow, and all might learn from him that this was certain and to be embraced [?]. For the Lord says:

"I do not desire the death of the sinner, so much as that he should turn and live." Through Cain, then, repentance for so great a crime was to be made plain to all, and with it an equally abundant pardon. In this way the good fruit borne by penitents would be shown to men as an encouragement from God, so that, seeing it, they might desire to gain salvation for themselves rather than death. Hence, as it were

his own accuser and judge, Cain [?] said that he had committed fratricide, and he deserved to hear from the Lord that, if the fruit of good works followed him from then on, he would without doubt receive forgiveness for so great a crime. He need no longer fear that anyone would put him to death.

Moreover, he also received a sign so that no one would kill him, and by heavenly sentence it was decreed that anyone who dared to lay hands on him would suffer twice seven punishments.
