Yet his repentance was found to be, as it were, feigned and not true, even as he hears from the Lord: "Whoever kills Cain will pay sevenfold vengeance."

So he deserved to receive the sign because of his repentance, provided that a fitting yield of good works now followed him. But we find no good fruit of repentance in him anywhere. Far from it: every kind of impiety sprang up instead from his descendants.

Those who came after him were heirs of their father's impiety and of the savagery of so great a crime. When blessed Noah preached to them, they refused to repent of their evils and persisted in wickedness. So they perished in the dreadful destruction of the flood. Only eight souls were spared at that time, born of the line of the saints, and they alone were found worthy to escape the storm of so great a peril.

There is a heresy that thinks the stars are fixed in the sky. It does not accept that at evening, by divine command, they suddenly come forth from storehouses and hidden places arranged by God, and at appointed hours recognize the course and the service laid upon their light.

Anyone who holds this view is found to be at odds with the catholic faith and foreign to it, and will be shown to share in pagan vanity and the empty opinion of the philosophers rather than in Christian knowledge.

For Scripture teaches the almighty power of God in such a way that it declares briefly that the stars gather together and move about from various storehouses. In part, God has given and lent them to adorn the sky and to serve night and light. At various intervals of the hours

they have been appointed to return, as it were, to their own places. Each day they are commanded to go out from those places and to return to them again, with an angel presiding over them and driving them on [?], so that they can in no way pass beyond their due course. Hence the outpoured clemency of Christ was to be made manifest to the whole human race, since in this world he has granted the same favor of his goodness to the just and the unjust. As Scripture declares:
"He makes his sun rise on the just and the unjust, and sends rain on the good and the evil"; and: "The stars," it says, "know their storehouses and their appointed course each day."

There are certain heretics who reject many things in the Old Testament, namely Solomon's Ecclesiastes. It is a book written in few sentences, yet it holds the whole treasure of heavenly knowledge for those who seek it.

The Savior himself testified that Solomon was wiser than all who came before him. So they read: "All things under heaven are vanity of vanities"; and: "I desired," he says, "to have" various things, as it is said; and: "God gave them to me," he says, "and behold, all is vanity of vanities." Yet afterward he adds that this alone comes from God: that a person should eat and drink and do good to his soul.

But if he had said that only this food and this drink, which are carnal, are useful in this world, and had proclaimed nothing else about the immortal life to come [?], then human labor would be spent in vain. So what the apostle says of certain people, "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die" [?]

[?] Such a heresy surely belongs to the pagans and the Epicureans, and it is like the life of cattle. Hence: "Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he has become like the senseless cattle." Solomon, then, declared both that the carnal life of men, with its many riches, is granted by God, and also that the future glory of the angels belongs to the earnest few who desire it and believe.

For if a rich man also does good works in this world, he must also obtain a share in the life to come there. Just as this earthly food has been given by God, so that heavenly food from the law is to be desired all the more. That food is the faith of Christ the Lord, which comes from the law and the prophets and is glorious to those who long for it. Mary chose it rather than Martha, as the Lord says that Mary had chosen the better portion, which would not be taken from her.

So when he said, "What is in the world is vanity of vanities," he was certainly declaring that these things pass away, in view of that future glory, which is surpassing and everlasting. As the apostle says: "For the form of this world passes away, and its glory." But if the form and life and honor and rank of this world will cease and be destroyed, then surely it is that heavenly and

angelic dignity that is to be desired. It will come to believers through the incarnation, passion and resurrection of Christ. It will not be temporal, carnal and perishable, like that of the Jews, who read by the letter, and of others like them who are perishing and expect nothing hereafter.

That is why the Lord says: "Work for the food that does not perish," that is, "that you believe in me, whom my Father sent." So Solomon was not speaking only of this carnal food and passing over the other. He was proclaiming the different kinds of food and the glory of holy men. First comes the carnal life of men in the present age, and after death comes that heavenly and angelic dignity for the just and faithful.

He declared this carnal life to be vain and temporal and bound to perish, namely the righteousness of the Jews and others like them. He did so in order that they might recognize it as a shadow and know that the life of the body is temporal and soon falls away compared with that heavenly and everlasting dignity. Of this food the prophet says: "Taste and see that the Lord is sweet."

There is a heresy that has doubts about the Song of Songs [?]. It likewise supposes that Solomon proclaimed it to men not by the divine Spirit but for the sake of human affairs and pleasures. In fact he taught the human race the truth of heavenly things by likening it to human things, as is done in the Gospels and everywhere in Scripture.
And so the divine presence of Christ in the flesh taught everyone in such a way as to stir them with divine love, soothe them with admonition, move them with mercy, and win them over with goodness.

As God he showed the way; as Father he admonished; as Shepherd he pointed out the pasture; as King he conquered the enemy and showed how to follow in his footsteps. So those who follow their brother, the Lord Christ who came in the flesh, may rejoice together with him in the triumph of immortal glory and heavenly reward.

That is why it is called the Song of Songs. What was formerly spoken in the law in part and in shadow was now, in the light of Christ's presence, to be laid open to believers as its fulfillment, once the mystery had been brought to completion and celebrated through the passion. When the shadow ceased, the truth of the heavenly light would shine out on every age, kindling the body and mind of man and stirring his understanding with heavenly love.

So vain men who have made themselves slaves to the lusts of the flesh either pretend that they cannot understand it or, if it is explained to them, scorn to learn. Since they are unwilling to recognize the power of the law, they are to be judged no differently from Jews or pagans.

Another heresy says that the commandment which Adam our father received is not to be accepted, and its followers think it had no force or usefulness. Yet without that commandment the law of Moses cannot be accepted, nor can the everlasting, outpoured and abundant grace of Christ be recognized.

For every man, set in the body, is instructed in a threefold way, to be taught and admonished by divine law. In the first age he is under the commandment, in the second under the law, in the third under the grace of the Savior. So the law is rather a reminder, given because of forgetfulness, of the original commandment that our father Adam first received from Christ in paradise. For so it is written.

And later, in the law, it says: "Do not forget the commandment of the Lord your God, depart from him, and perish." So the law is a reminder and confirmation of that first commandment. And both the commandment and the law proclaim the full goodness of Christ's grace and his saving presence. That is why the Lord says: "Behold, I who spoke in the prophets am here."

So the ancients who lived under the commandment are greater. They did not forget it, and they proclaimed to their descendants the grace of Christ the Savior and his mystery. When the Jews forgot it, the reminder of the written letter followed in turn, so that even in the letter people might hope for the spiritual knowledge of Christ and his bodily presence, which would enlighten the world.

So the law of Moses proclaimed one thing in the sound of its words and another hidden within, since it contained the saving mystery of Christ. Therefore no one ought to accept or believe the commandment without the law, or the law without the commandment, or the grace of Christ without the law and the commandment.

There are certain heretics who read in Scripture that the Lord said, "Let us make man in our image and likeness," and fall into no small madness. First, they do not know what the image of God is and what the likeness is. And since they do not know what the image of God is by nature, as something proper to him, and what it is by appointment, through grace, they claim for themselves no small and proud dignity.

For the image of God is the soul of every man, made from nothing. But the likeness lies in faith and life [?]: unless it is recognized by God, it cannot be called an image like God. And when someone thinks himself something more, he incurs the charge of presumption rather than gaining the merit of dignity.
For when this soul is found sinning and is known to be liable to judgment and held for it, how can it be the natural image of God, when it is plainly enslaved to various sins?

There can be no other natural image of God, divine and proper to the Father, whether of an angel or a man, except Christ, God, the Son of God. By natural property he is the image of the Father's eternal substance, undivided from it, begotten in the proper sense. He was not created from nothing in the condition of a servant, as man and angel are.

So Scripture declared that the soul of all pagans, Jews, heretics and all people can be called the image of God, because of their common origin, and it proclaimed that its substance is of one and the same nature. But it declared that the likeness belongs not to all, but only to the saints and to Christians.

These persevere in faith, in their way of life and in good works, and they are promised that they will obtain the heavenly rewards of the angels in the future. Such were the patriarchs, prophets, priests, judges, apostles, evangelists and martyrs. They believed in the Trinity and persevered in an excellent life, and the Lord declares that they will be joined to the glory of the angels.

For the true likeness is recognized by the teaching of the law, by faith, by one's way of life, by zeal and by works. A person who agrees with the divine law of the God who made him and fulfills the precepts he laid down may hope to obtain from him a share in the heavenly kingdom. As the apostle says:

"Our citizenship is in heaven"; and the Lord says again: "Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven." He was also showing that on the day of judgment they would be like angels, when the Lord says again of the heavenly kingdom: "Come, receive the kingdom that has been prepared for you from the foundation of the world."

So the likeness is shown to exist through faith in the Holy Trinity, a good life, and the works that follow, so that when they depart this life they may receive the promised share in the dignity of the angels. As John says: "Then we shall be like him"; and the Lord: "Be like your Father."

There are certain heretics who say: "Why did God not always speak in one way? Why did he preach to the human race in various ways and languages?" Yet he spoke and appeared to men according to their capacity, as far as they were able to see, grasp and hear.

So once man had been cast out of paradise and had put on death, God no longer appeared as he had before. Instead he spoke from heaven, and his voice was heard and heeded. In the course of time he also deigned to appear, as he did to the most blessed patriarch Abraham and to others in turn. Under Moses he appeared in various forms, and on Mount Sinai he showed what belonged to fear and to error [?];

and afterward, in the figure of an angel and in the form of a man, with signs going before of his future incarnation, he proclaimed his clemency toward all. The Lord also showed himself to the just in visions and dreams, as it is written. But afterward he appeared in the incarnation and bore witness to the Jews, proclaiming what he had said before through the prophets.

Since, then, people differed in their capacity to see the Lord, he acted like a good physician and gave different remedies for men's infirmities as each illness required. So at the end he gave more medicine to a world that was sick. In this way the surpassing strength of those first men was shown, and the dangerous weakness of our generation was made known. As the Lord says: "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick."

So those earlier men who believed when they heard, such as Seth, Enoch, Noah and the rest, are greater than we are. We hear and read of the mercy of Christ the Lord and his abundant goodness, and yet we despise it.

For the sake of the Jews he also spoke in other languages, so that this might be fulfilled: "In other tongues and with other lips I will speak to this people, and even so they will not believe, says the Lord." For through Isaiah he says: "I will send my word into Achaia."

Another heresy, when it reads of the four living creatures in the prophets, falls into no small error. It supposes that animals of various shapes praised God, not knowing that irrational creatures, that is, creatures incapable of reason, cannot offer praise to God as men can.

For God does not seek the praise of cattle. It was not cattle that were made in the image of God; God created rational men and appointed them for this. But since this is a vision proclaimed by the prophets through the divine Spirit, it foretold four different virtues and different struggles of holy peoples that were to come into the world, with different teachings and virtues and differing heights of excellence.

These are the lion, the calf, the man and the eagle, and their different teachings and shining merits were foreshadowed in them. First, royal authority would be seen in the patriarchs; then the rich fruit of heavenly knowledge in the prophets; and in the priests strong labor and persistent struggle.

In the apostles a lofty flight into heaven and eminent dignity would be displayed. So what the diversity of forms had foretold, namely the heavenly merits of different virtues, would be made manifest in the world when Christ was present, as gifts granted by the Lord and Savior himself.

For in the lion we recognize the kingship of strength, in the calf surpassing labor, in the man unceasing suffering, and in the eagle lofty flight. These belong to those who strive and serve as soldiers. As the apostle says: "Our citizenship is in heaven"; and: "We shall be caught up into heaven and shall be with Christ forever," he says. And the Lord deigned to say: "Father, where I am, I wish these also to be with me."

There are certain heretics who have doubts about the day of the Epiphany of the Lord and Savior, which is celebrated on the eighth day before the Ides of January. They say that they should celebrate only the Lord's birthday, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, and not the day of Epiphany. They do not know that under the law and according to [?] the Savior fulfilled all things in and through himself in the flesh: he was born on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, and he also appeared, as he appeared to the magi twelve days later [?] in the temple. So it was not a shadow but what was true that appeared, and so he was worshiped by the magi.

For our salvation these four annual days of greater festival have been established in order. First is the day on which he was born. Next is the day on which he appeared, that is, twelve days later. After that is the day on which he suffered, at Passover. Last is the day on which he ascended into heaven, around Pentecost, which is the crowning of the victor.

So whoever ignores one of these and passes it over may come to doubt the other days as well, since he does not have the fullness of truth. For in this way, across the four seasons of each year, different joys have sprung up for us from Christ the Lord: first the day on which he was born, then the day on which he appeared, third the day on which he suffered, rose again and was seen, and fourth the day on which he ascended into heaven.

So we should celebrate these days throughout the year without interruption, all rejoicing together, and keep them whole and inviolate. Some, however, think that the day of Epiphany is the day of the baptism, and others that it is the day of the transfiguration on the mountain.

There are other heretics who are ignorant of the precepts of the law that were given through Moses in Leviticus. These were spoken to the Jews in a fleshly sense and have been revealed spiritually in our time. Not knowing this, these heretics pass over the full scheme of the festivals and their number, which is of heavenly benefit. They do not know what they are celebrating, and they think that Moses gave commands only about sabbaths, Passover and unleavened bread, and not about the eight festivals that the catholic church recognizes and keeps.

For blessed Moses speaks to the Jewish people in this way: first about the new moon and the sabbaths, second about Passover, third about unleavened bread, fourth about the sheaves, and fifth about the blowing of trumpets, which in Greek are called salpinges. The Jews celebrate these solemnly through the year. Sixth comes the fast, seventh the building of tabernacles, and the eighth is the last gathering and completion of all, the fullness of the crops and the vintage of the fruits in the month of October.

The Jews celebrate this sequence across eight months according to the letter, but it can also be understood spiritually. Beginning in the month of March and running to the eighth month, that is October, everything is brought to completion in order by Christ the Lord. These are pledges full of eternal salvation, to be fulfilled and proven in the faith and works of Christianity.

At that time the Jews were commanded to offer God various gifts in these months, so that, turning away from idols, they might know that all these things were to be offered to God. Even so, the gifts held signs of a spiritual offering. The eighth signified the perfection of the virtues, that is, the full grace of the fruits of the Lord's day. Through faith in the Lord's resurrection, people would obtain an immortal reward and a pledge that they would attain the dignity of angels. They would no longer offer the gifts of an earthly offering, that is, the sacrifices of a fleshly life. Instead they hoped to obtain from Christ the Lord, the Savior, a share in heavenly glory.

For they offered yearly gifts eight times and recognized the fullness of the eighth day, namely the Lord's day. Girded with the strength of the divine Spirit, that is, endowed with the highest perfection, they did not despair, when they departed from this world, of attaining there the promised glory of the resurrection and being joined to the fellowship of heavenly dignity. As the Lord deigned to say: "Then you will be like the angels." He was proclaiming this to all the righteous and perfect, and David said the same in the psalms he headed "for the eighth."

There are heretics who, like the Jews, reject the translation of the seventy-two holy and very wise men. Instead they accept the edition of Aquila, a single man from Pontus, who made his translation many years later. Because at that time pressing necessity compelled the seventy-two to leave certain things out, people think they produced a discordant text. Some, especially Jews, praise Aquila as if he had understood more, since he did not render what concerns the Father and the Son as those earlier translators rendered the law.

For the seventy-two said: "Against the Lord, and against his Christ"; but Aquila said: "Against the Lord, and against his anointed one." Again, the seventy-two said: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be God with us." But Aquila said: "Behold, a young woman shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be Mighty among men."

If these readings are taken in a devout sense, so that no one is strong and mighty except Christ, God, the Son of God, then the reader understands rightly. But if the reader has doubts about him, such an edition must be rejected and spurned. This is why the Jews do not use the translation of the seventy-two, who held the right belief about the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit and proclaimed one substance, divinity and majesty. They use Aquila's instead, because he did not think rightly about the Son of God and spoke of him as if he were a prophet.

For this reason Aquila's renderings are never placed in the middle of the books but are set to the right and left, and most people read them as contrary to the truth and lacking its fullness. The catholic church reads the decisions and judgments of the seventy-two, and it has always held and kept them without hesitation. Aquila's version it regards and judges as superfluous.

This translation of the seventy-two was published for everyone under Ptolemy, king of the Egyptians, who came after Alexander of Macedon. It was commissioned from the Jewish people in Jerusalem at a time when not many Jews lived there, for they were by then subject to the Egyptian king. Ptolemy himself asked them to send translators to Alexandria.
When the seventy-two wise and prudent men, the translators, had come, they translated the Hebrew language into Greek at the king's command and published it in Greek letters, and so it was done.

When Ptolemy king of Egypt had received them, he wanted to test whether the scripture that the Jews read was divine. So he ordered each of them to be shut in a separate room and to see no one except the scribe who took down the translator's dictation.

Afterwards he received the translations of all of them each day. When he found that all their versions agreed as one, he ordered the translation to be copied out and placed in the temple. In this way philosophers, poets and historians coming from Achaia, from Greece and from other provinces who wished to read it would not be denied the chance.

From this source above all, philosophers, poets, orators and historians took their material and turned it as they pleased to the lies of their paganism. They taught the untrained minds of children under other names and hurried to make the divine law of God void for the world. They planted the seeds of impiety in the sound of their words and in dangerous opinions. It was because of them that the Lord said they were thieves and robbers, to be recognized as such in everything and by everyone.

There is a heresy which, again after Aquila, accepts the translation of the Thirty men. It does not accept that of those most blessed seventy-two, who held a whole and unblemished belief about the Trinity and, in translating the scriptures, handed down to the catholic church its surest foundations.
Because these thirty followed Aquila in many things, the catholic church does not accept their translation either, and it is not included among the authentic books.

There is also a heresy that wishes to follow the translation of the Six men, published later, rather than that of the earlier and holy seventy-two. Since these people want to interpret the decisions and judgments of the seventy-two in other ways, they fall into no small error and likewise hold different views about the catholic faith.

There are other heretics who likewise follow the translation of Theodotion and Symmachus, which renders the text differently. They do not follow that of the most blessed earlier translators, which the catholic church reveres and proclaims.

There is another heresy that wishes to follow the books found in a jar. These were brought out after the captivity and after the burning, and they do not agree with the first translation made by the holy men. But the catholic church reads, reveres and proclaims the translation of the seventy-two, and it despises and rejects the others as superfluous and contrary to so great an edition.

There are certain heretics who do not understand what scripture says: "You shall not curse foreign gods." They observe this command in the belief that it was said about the vain gods of the pagans. Holding this view, they do no small harm to their own salvation.

For Moses says: "You shall destroy their temples, you shall break their idols." Most blessed Abraham was justified by breaking idols. Gideon burned and broke idols by night and so earned from the Lord Christ such great strength that with a few men he conquered countless enemies. All the righteous did the same, such as blessed Elijah and others. How then can this foolish man think that the verse was spoken about the vain idols and that they must not be cursed? For David says: "Let those who worship them become like them."

So when scripture says here that foreign gods are not to be cursed, it means the righteous who from the beginning of the world have practiced true piety. That is, the angels and the other saints devoted to the true faith are not to be cursed.

All the righteous cursed idols and broke them and earned grace by doing so, as Moses did when he came down from Mount Sinai. And Christ's messengers are gods, as Moses was to Pharaoh and the Egyptians. For scripture cries out:

"I said, you are gods." There is no doubt that this means those who worship the holy and adorable Trinity and preach it with strong faith. All of these are righteous, truly blessed and holy, and they are recognized as gods, namely as the gods of unbelievers. For the Lord says: "Those to whom the word of God came" [?]. Those through whom the word was preached were themselves called the gods of unbelievers, like Paul, Barnabas, and Moses before Pharaoh. They are not to be cursed

but praised, honored and glorified in every way, as David said: "But he glorifies those who fear the Lord"; and the Lord said: "Those who glorify me I will glorify." So these heretics, not understanding the force of the scriptures, side with paganism by keeping to the letter, and they are found to be strangers to Christianity.

Because the Jews did not believe the righteous prophets and others like them, the Lord through scripture judged them to be foreigners too, just like the pagans. So the command was given that they should not curse their teachers and prophets, the righteous and the others.

There are certain heretics who read in Genesis about Melchizedek, priest and king, who lived in the city then called Salem in the time of the most blessed patriarch Abraham. Scripture says of him that he was born without father and without mother, [?] although

it is wrong to understand it in this way. For scripture did not deny that he was born by fleshly generation. It declared that he was not born of righteous parents. By natural zeal and from the original commandment he earned so great a knowledge of Christ that, through the commandment and by his own zeal, he came to recognize the greater mysteries of Christ that were to be offered, things he had not heard from his parents. For the Lord says through the prophets: "Behold, I make new things"; and: "Before they come, they have been announced to you"; and: "Do not remember the former things," meaning the things spoken in a fleshly sense in the law.

And the Savior says: "What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit." So when scripture says of Melchizedek that he was born without father and without mother, it declares that he searched out the truth without the tradition and teaching of his parents. It shows that he was by nature strong and capable of heavenly wisdom, that is, attentive through the commandment to the mystery of Christ.

The apostle knew that human nature is capable of heavenly knowledge and piety in every respect, and he preached it in this way: "For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature the things of the law,

these, though they do not have the law, are a law to themselves. They show the work of the law written in their hearts," and so on. The Lord said the same to Peter: flesh and blood had not revealed it to him, but the Father who is in heaven. In this he pointed to faith in the Lord, the Savior. So the Lord himself says again: "Unless someone is reborn of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven." And again in the law:

"Those who said to father and mother, 'We do not know you,' have kept my commandment," says the Lord. He does not mean that being begotten by parents is to be hated. He means that their pagan impiety must be spurned and condemned in every way. [?] he praised, since he says: "If anyone does not renounce all that is his, he will not be worthy of the kingdom of heaven." So this blessed

Melchizedek, though born of foreigners, that is, of the impious Canaanites, despised his parents' impiety. By his own zeal he was capable of the divine and heavenly law, as the image of God. Having sought out the mystery of Christ and rejected his impious parents, he earned not only the knowledge of Christ the Lord beforehand through the commandment but also the privilege of celebrating his heavenly mystery, beholding and understanding it. This is why the apostle said to the baptized:

"But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit." At that time, then, the two peoples of Melchizedek and Abraham were joined in a single fellowship, in a fitting harmony of uncircumcision and circumcision. Melchizedek represented the Christians,

as we live and celebrate in all things, while Abraham was a figure of the circumcision of the Jews, which is subject to the faith of Christ and serves his heavenly and saving mystery. So blessed Abraham was subject to Melchizedek the great priest and did not hesitate even to offer him tithes from his possessions [?], as to the king and priest of God. In the same way, the unteachable Jews are now subject to us. They are meant to want to learn and gradually come to know from us the mysteries of Christ from the law and the prophets, and in his passion to hope for heavenly knowledge drawn from the law and the prophets alike.

There are some who read in Zechariah what he says: "The fast on the fourth day, and the fast on the fifth, and the fast on the seventh, and the fast on the tenth shall be joy and gladness for the house of Israel." What then? If someone wishes to fast every week or for many months, will he incur condemnation?

Far from it. On the contrary, he will deserve greater praise, as many prophets did and very many righteous people do every day. When scripture speaks of four fasts, it seems to decree four days of fasting. Yet it did not tell us which month or which year. It proclaimed the fasts without qualification so that we would recognize that the mysteries of Christianity are announced in these four fasts.

For four fasts are celebrated in the church through the year: first at the Nativity, then at Easter, third at the Ascension and fourth at Pentecost. One must fast at the Nativity of the Lord, the Savior, and then at Easter during Lent. Likewise one fasts at the Ascension into heaven, on the fortieth day after Easter, and from then until Pentecost for ten days, or afterwards.

The blessed apostles did this after the Ascension, persevering in fasting and prayer. As it is written, they earned at Pentecost the fullness of the divine Spirit and the perfection of power. The divine Spirit flowed over them in abundance, and now, equipped with heavenly arms, they set aside all the doubt they had felt before. Afterwards they hurried every day to become invincible teachers and glorious martyrs of the Lord himself, teaching Jews and pagans

and proving to them from the law and the prophets, by the prophets' testimonies, that Christ is everywhere God, eternal with the Father, and announcing to the whole world his saving presence in the flesh. Others think that scripture was speaking of the four seasons of each year.

Others claim that it spoke of Noah: first when he heard and believed, then when he built the ark, later when he entered it, and fourth when he came out of the ark. Some of the Jews, however, think that scripture spoke of Israel. First the people heard through Moses in Egypt and believed at that time, and they were freed from Pharaoh and the Egyptians. Next they went out of Egypt. Third, they went to the mountain and received the law from the Lord, the Savior. Fourth, they entered the promised land.

But not all of them entered it, as it is written. Only two did, Joshua and Caleb, as scripture says. Still others have said that these four fasts are enjoined on the church in the four books of Moses. First, in Genesis, God made all things and man, as it is written. Second, in Exodus, everyone who believes in Christ, God, will go out freed from darkness. Third, in Leviticus, he offers various sacrifices, all of which are mysteries of Christianity. Fourth, after the offering of spiritual gifts, every believer earns the right to be enrolled in the book of Numbers. As the Lord says: "Rejoice, because your names are written in the book of heaven."

That is why David says of the Jews: "Let them be blotted out of the book, and not be written with the righteous." And he says again: "And in your book those who believe in you shall be written." We should also relate these fasts to the four gospels [?], to the patriarchs, prophets, priests and apostles, whose example must be fulfilled in us. First the faith of the patriarchs is proclaimed, then the virtue of the prophets, third the labor of the priests, and fourth the perfection of the apostles' invincible struggle. These different virtues flourish together, each joined to its own time. As they teach people, they supply many kinds of joy and delight to those who desire and receive them.

There are heretics who read in Solomon: "Sixty queens, and eighty concubines, and maidens without number." They think he gave these numbers for the sake of the women, the girls and the concubines. Those who hold this view are judged unfruitful, or rather like impious pagans and uneducated, untaught Jews.

They do not know that these words were spoken by Solomon to be reasoned out and understood spiritually. They showed that in the majesty and power of Christ the human race would receive various gifts of grace. These gifts would be imparted by Christ at different times according to people's will and the capacity of those who desire them. God does not refuse an equal grace. Rather, the Lord himself grants and confers on those who seek earnestly as much as their will is known to be able to receive. As the blessed apostle Peter says: "In truth I have found that God shows no partiality." And the apostle Paul

says likewise: "God," he says, "shows no partiality to anyone." So each person is granted and given by God, Christ, every day according to his will, according to what he receives and desires. Solomon, then, has announced to us various dignities and various glories. Under the commandment, the law and the grace of Christ, and in every age, that is, the first, the second and the last, various gifts of dignity have been conferred on the peoples according to their merits: first on the earliest people, then on that of the Jews, and third on that of the Christians.
For when we are taught by those earlier ones who lived before the Jews, we see that in the presence of Christ, God, a diverse grace is poured out every day on those who receive and seek it.

It is clear that some souls are called to rule, others to union, and others to growth in the maturity of age, all into union with the coming faith of Christ the Lord. As the apostle says: "Whoever is joined to Christ the Lord is one body." Where the word "queen" is used, the high excellence of nobility in the heavenly kingdom is shown. So also the Lord, proclaiming that many are called, announces that few will be chosen, and in these a threefold dignity of virtue shines forth.

In the gospel too the Lord said to that man: "If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and come, follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven." But the man, it says, went away sad, as it is written.

So although this happened earlier in a general way, according to the division of times and peoples, still a threefold grace and dignity shines out in the presence of Christ. Some were shown to be perfect, others to be following, and others to be going to follow later. They will not all have one kind of dignity, that is, of finding the heavenly kingdom. Instead each will receive a fitting reward according to his faith and labor and the different struggles he has faced. As the Lord says: "There are many mansions with my Father."

That is why David praises in every way the soul that is called to rule, teaching: "The queen stood at your right hand." He urges another soul to follow as well: "Hear, daughter, and see, and forget your father's house, and the king will desire your beauty."

It is reasonable, then, to recognize that in the life to come some will be assigned to the kingdom, others to paradise, and others to life and the forgiveness of sins. This is not denied to those who run and are willing, even now, as they should be. But the Lord will not grant these things to those who are careless and do not run the race rightly.

There is a heresy which thinks that Joshua son of Nun circumcised the Jewish people with stone knives. Neither the nature of things allows this, nor do power or reason make it believable. The Jews were more likely to be put in danger by this than healed. Nothing, it is true, is impossible to the power of God, yet the nature of things does not allow this, nor does reason make it believable.

So Scripture does not say that the Jews were circumcised with stone knives. It means the very hard and stony minds of the pagans. These minds had once been given over to impiety. Afterwards, however, the pagans believed in the Lord and lost their stony minds, and they were found worthy, once they had themselves been circumcised by the word of God and made strong by a mind and teaching now heavenly, to circumcise the Jews. That is, they were worthy to instil in them the saving knowledge of Christ, proclaiming it from the Law and the Prophets and proving it on every side.

For indeed the Jews are circumcised every day by those who were formerly Gentiles. That is, they are taught from the Law and the Prophets about faith in Christ, the Lord and Savior [?]. If they believe, they too will receive the remedy of salvation. But if they persist in the hardness of a stony mind, they will be held for eternal judgment.

This is why the Lord too, faced with their stubborn opposition, said that their sons, that is, the pagans themselves, would be their judges and teachers. He meant the people of the Gentiles, who once lived with a stony mind but afterwards, through faith in Christ, were found worthy to attain saving knowledge.

Israel, however, running according to the law, as it is written, could not attain the power of the law, because it hurried to run on the basis of works rather than faith. For Jacob says that he will be the hope of the Gentiles, not of the Jews. So all the Gentiles must first believe. Only then will the Jews learn from those same Gentiles, hear the teaching of Christ the Lord from the Law and the Prophets, and so give their assent, so that this may be fulfilled: "Until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in, and so all Israel will be saved," as it is written. Another prophet says: "Take away from them the heart of stone, O Lord, and give them a heart of flesh." And the Lord says: "If these keep silent, the stones will cry out."

There is another heresy which thinks that the breath Adam received was as great as the Spirit Christ granted to the apostles after the resurrection. It does not know that the breath is a grace of modest power, which many possess, for hearing the law of God. The Spirit, by contrast, is the fullness of perfection.

So the breath is given from infancy, and to catechumens as well. The Spirit, however, comes as doctrine and faith grow. It is the full grace of God given in saving baptism, so that you may understand and go on to greater knowledge. This is why whoever is baptized into the Trinity receives, after baptism, the Spirit, as the apostles did, and no longer merely the breath.

For the breath is common to all, but the Spirit belongs to few. It belongs to the faithful, to believers and learners, and to those who advance, as it were, from honor to honor and from glory to glory towards greater, heavenly knowledge and grace. As the apostle says, we proceed from faith to faith, and we hasten to go forward from glory to glory.

This is why he himself says: "The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly." Human nature is thus shown to have some share in Christ's gift and not to be wholly a stranger to it; even the catechumen is not left out. Yet faith and doctrine, zeal and an outstanding life are seen to abound only by the will of the few faithful who earnestly desire them. As the Lord says: "To the one who has, more will be given, and more will be added to him; but from the one who has not, even what he seems to have will be taken away." This is what happened to the Jew, and likewise to very many others.

There is a heresy which, when it hears in the prophet Zechariah of the surveyor's measuring line, of which the blessed prophet David had also spoken, and of how an angel holding it went to measure Jerusalem, supposes that Scripture spoke literally. But the point was not to measure Jerusalem, which was about to be handed over to its enemies. Rather, the angel was announcing the coming election of those who believe rightly, the few who are perfect, as it was said: "Many are called, but few are chosen."

So Jerusalem was measured with the surveyor's line. That is, both earlier, when the faithful were few, and after faith in Christ came, a coming election of a few of the catholic faith was proclaimed in the world. The apostle says this too: "There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may be made manifest." The cord of inheritance, then, is woven of a threefold power, that is, of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. When this union is received in one and the same faith and belief, the catholic church recognizes it as a unity of equality and truth, to be held together, and as a power to be worshipped. It is not preached as something to be believed of a substance differing in majesty or quality, as certain heretics suppose.

The Lord also deigned to say this: "Do you think that the Son of Man, when he comes, will find faith on the earth?" For the prophet had earlier announced that faith was then found among few, and after the presence of Christ, his passion and resurrection [?], it was announced by divine sentence that people would fall away. Such are the heretics of today who depart from the Holy Spirit or from the Son and, going astray, every

day preach a difference of majesty and an inequality of power. In this matter, then, we must recognize that the cord, as Solomon says, being threefold, will not be broken. We must also believe that the Son is of the divine substance and of the Father's own, and likewise the Holy Spirit, who is joined to the Father in all things and must be known and worshipped by all. In this union of baptism, then, the Savior deigned to confirm us, commanding: "Go and baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit."

When we join the Son to the Father, and the Spirit with the Son and the Father, we are known to be on the way to this salvation. For we know that the remedy of salvation will come to the human race from nowhere else than from this faith. That is why we rejoice in this union of the holy and adorable Trinity. In it, in times past, Adam our father, Noah, Abraham, Moses and the prophets, the priests, the judges, and the apostles and evangelists alike, preaching it, were found worthy to attain the dignity of angels. In it the catholic church also exults, preaching and teaching it every day, and as it destroys all this pagan impiety and Jewish iniquity day by day, it exults with all joy.

Now if the threefold cord is to be understood as first the commandment, then the law in the middle period, and then the grace of the Savior, that reading is of no small use. Or if someone wishes to take it as faith, hope and love, as the blessed apostle said, this too gives no small understanding to the more prudent and to the many who desire spiritual things.

There are certain heretics who think that ravens brought blessed Elijah meat to eat in the evening and bread in the morning. They do not consider that the holy and most blessed prophet never ate meat at all, for he had renounced all such food by voluntary abstinence. For this reason he was found worthy to receive from God the honor of such great dignity that he was caught up on high into paradise, to be placed there with all the saints.

If someone speaks of bread, it is reasonable enough that the ravens brought it to him; but in the case of meat this is found to be unfitting. For in this episode the beastly cruelty of the men who pursued the most blessed prophet was displayed, while in the birds, that is, the ravens, great gentleness and mildness were shown. These birds lacked human reason. They were not rational images of God, but merely birds created with senses, like cattle. Yet in them, to the shame of men, of the Jews and of the king who pursued the prophet with the most wicked intent, a recognition and a gentleness of feeling planted within them was displayed in the work of so great a service, rendered daily to the blessed prophet. In those birds, then, there was found to be rather a kind of reason of gentleness, granted by God through some impulse, as though they were rational.

For all created things of this kind are subject by the Lord to man, as king, as a rational being and as lord of the world and of all cattle, birds and serpents too, as is written and shown in the book of Genesis.

There is a heresy which is greatly disturbed when it reads in the prophet Isaiah that the Cherubim and Seraphim, two living creatures with six wings, covered the face of God with two wings and his feet with two, and with two cried out in a lofty voice, praising God. Now seeking the historical sense, now searching out the intelligible meaning, its followers wear themselves out with all kinds of uncertainty. Yet the literal sense is of no small use, and in the intelligible meaning the heavenly knowledge of Christ resounds.

According to the letter, first of all, Scripture, by teaching that God is invisible, condemned pagan impiety everywhere, since the pagans' impious writings proclaim him to be visible and composite. It then also condemned the impiety of the Jews. It taught this so that they too would not be covered with the same blindness as the impious Gentiles and perish with their senses corrupted.

But here there was also to be announced the unbelief of the Jews of a future time, in the presence of Christ, and the veiling of the mystery. Covered with excessive blindness, they would afterwards believe neither the prophet nor the Lord himself, when, sent to the people, he preaches plainly: "With the ear you will hear, and with the eye you will see, and you will not perceive." Covered with darkness, they would not recognize the light of eternal salvation, that is, the presence of Christ in the flesh, and that is just what happened.

The apostle taught this, affirming that a veil lies over their hearts to this day, which will not be lifted until they believe in Christ the Savior. But when they are converted, that is, when they believe in Christ the Lord, the veil will be taken from their hearts. And there is no doubt that the two living creatures announced, the Cherubim and Seraphim, are the Law and the Prophets, the witnesses of Christ and the teachers of the world.

They veiled the face and feet of the Lord, [?] because the mystery was taught in parables, likenesses and riddles, as it is written: "I will open my mouth in a parable"; and David says: "Unveil my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law"; and the apostle says: "The Father revealed his Son to me," that is, showing him from the Law and the Prophets.

They had six wings. With two they covered the face, with two the feet, and with two they cried out. The face and feet were covered so that when Scripture speaks of the Lord's face and feet, what is above and below, no one would suppose that God has length and breadth. For the height, the depth, the breadth and the length of God cannot be known or worthily found out by any creature, least of all by man, nor can anyone's human senses grasp them. He even created and completed the vast nature of the elements, so how much more must he who is known to have made such things surpass them in every way? He is known only through faith;

for "power," it says, "is made perfect in weakness," in likenesses and riddles, and there it is found. And when so great an immensity of God is spoken of and announced, it is sung and preached by two wings, that is, by the Cherubim and Seraphim, the Law and the Prophets. The crying of the two wings day and night, that is, both here and in the age to come, is the belief of the human heart and the confession of the mouth, which is found never to cease and resounds every day. It was sung then by the angels and preached in the world by men, so that what they could not see in height, depth, breadth and length, they might believe with the heart and confess with the mouth, singing with unceasing voice and rejoicing at all times.

That the divine substance, in its quality and nature, is invisible and cannot be contained is shown in the Law and the Prophets, and John says: "No one has ever seen God." He did not say "believed", but "seen". So the Lord granted only the power of believing and the confidence of confessing, so that his unspeakable power, revealed in the frailty of the flesh, might be known. For the Lord everywhere holds out to men the faith in him, which he himself had given beforehand and afterwards confirmed by his presence.

The fourfold forms of the Cherubim and Seraphim, that is, of the lion, the calf, the man and the eagle, are the various and mighty contests of the saints and of their virtues alike, showing their excellent and varied dignity. These are the patriarchs and prophets, the priests and apostles, joined likewise with the martyrs. In them such abounding faith and love of Christ were known from the first. Afterwards, because the circumstances of the time required it, an unequal teaching was seen in some. Yet an equal glory of faith and contest was shown in the union of their various virtues, granted and bestowed by Christ, and it was to be known among all the Christian people;

so that what we cannot see, nor worthily define with human senses, we may believe in our hearts and confess confidently with our mouths. By the power of these two wings we must never cease to proclaim this joy to Jews and Gentiles, and by these powers we must fly up on high, hoping for heavenly things, where Christ is Lord, as the apostle says. Nor should we doubt that by this belief we can attain everlasting salvation, as the same apostle teaches: "If you believe in your heart and confess that Christ the Lord and Savior, crucified in the body, has risen, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation."

So he says of Christ the Lord that the divine substance of his nature does not consist in sight or measure or any composition, but is brought to completion, overflowing, in the faith and confession of our virtue. "To know," he says, "what is the breadth and length, the height and depth," that is, the most exalted and incomprehensible grace and power of Christ God, is not something human frailty [?] can set forth with power. But he taught that what the human mind cannot express can easily be attained in faith and through faith.

There are some who suppose [?] that blessed Isaiah [?], after the confession of the sinful people and the prayer he had poured out as a suppliant to God, was visited by one of the Cherubim, sent to the prophet by the Lord. They hold that it took a coal with tongs, touched his lips and said to him: "Behold, now you are cleansed." They think that either one of the angels or one of the living creatures came to him, took fire with the tongs and cleansed the most blessed prophet. But this reading does not convey much saving knowledge. For here, when it speaks of "one living creature of the Cherubim or Seraphim", it means one of the two testaments. From these flowed the patriarchs, priests, prophets and apostles, who showed the whole world the grace that was to come and ministered gifts shining with fourfold power to those who received them for the heavenly contests.

For when it speaks of Cherubim or Seraphim, it means the fullness of knowledge, and it names a fiery power that passes through all things. These, then, having the fullness of spiritual knowledge and holding the riches of the mystery of Christ, at the Lord's command hand down and deliver to us various teachings, proclaiming them likewise to every age without any pause. One of them was sent to the prophet Isaiah to announce this teaching of Christ: that the Savior was to come in the flesh and would bring to believers the abundant grace of the divine Spirit.

So Isaiah had received from the patriarchs, from the law and from the prophets before him a stronger grace, that is, a fuller power of the divine Spirit, from those who came before him, so that he might announce to the world, as a grace, the mystery of Christ, that is, of his incarnation. That is why the Lord said to some: "O you who are hard of heart and foolish of mind, why do you not see that everything the Law and the Prophets foretold would happen to the Son of Man had to be fulfilled?"

For he meant that blessed Isaiah received from the patriarchs and the law, so that, taught by them, he might boldly preach the presence of Christ in the flesh. And the fire which the angel is said to have taken and used to cleanse his lips certainly showed the grace of the divine Spirit granted to him by the Lord, as he says: "I came to cast fire upon the world, and how I wish it were soon kindled!" By the tongs, that is, by the iron, he meant its unconquerable and indeed divine nature and power. For the body of Christ was created and perfected in the womb of the holy Virgin by the divine Spirit and divine power, as it is written: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of God will overshadow you," [?] so that, appearing in that body, he might conquer all things and be overcome by none.

For just as all things are tamed and subdued by iron, from which the sword too is made, so, as it has been said, the word of the Lord is like a two-edged sword, which can tame all things but can be tamed by none. And after his passion, at his resurrection, he was to give the blessed apostles the invincible power of the divine Spirit, as it is written: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me," and so on. Blessed Peter, too, speaking to the Jews about the promise received from the Father, says: "He has poured out this grace, which you see and hear today." And just as we know that tongs are shaped by fire, so we know that the Lord's body was formed by the divine Spirit, and that in that body he gave his own people the promised grace and invincible power, as he says:

"I have given you power to tread upon all the might of the enemy." And the apostle says: "Who will separate us from the love of Christ?" By these gifts, as has been said, the divine Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles' hands to all who now believe in this world, those who believe in Christ the Lord, the Savior.

The two living creatures are taken to be these two testaments, of the Law and the Prophets, standing beside the Lord, as the apostles saw on the mountain. Yet it will also be reasonable to understand the two creatures in another way. The first is the commandment that was given in the beginning, which can also be understood spiritually, as it is written, and which the Savior did not abolish but rather confirmed. The second creature contained the teaching of Christ, that is, faith in him, the grace of his incarnation, and the mystery of his testament, his passion and his resurrection.

So the law of the letter is placed in the middle, between the commandment and grace. If it is understood rightly, it is accepted as agreeing in many things with what concerns Christ. But if anyone thinks he will be saved by fleshly justification, the law is judged to be rejected. For before the law, that is, three thousand seven hundred years earlier, those earlier righteous men lived under the commandment. They worshipped the blessed Trinity and handed it on to their sons and kin, preached about the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit to the world, and announced the mystery of Christ the Lord from that most ancient commandment.

The law, then, is a reminder of the commandment. It is joined to the commandment in the faith that worships the Trinity, and yet certain parts of it are set apart because of Jewish and fleshly justification. The prophets had already destroyed these parts, the Savior rejected them, and the apostles forbade people to be circumcised. So the law came down from the commandment for a time, because fleshly circumstances required it. But the grace of Christ, that is, the mystery of his incarnation, passion and resurrection, of faith in him and of his ascension into heaven, was known before the law by all the righteous. It was not hidden from those who sought and received it, such as Enoch, Noah and Melchizedek, Jacob and the other righteous and most blessed patriarchs, and the others who lived before the law of Moses. They were placed under the commandment and justified by the Lord in all things.

Faith in Christ is also called a law, as the apostle says: "Through [?] the law of the faith of Christ"; the fleshly law is the justification of the Jews. And although the commandment is not thought to be law, yet because it is spoken and decreed by a lord to a servant, it has the character of law. The one who receives it may choose as he wishes: either to keep it as a friend and faithful one, or to despise it as a servant placed under the law. So the Savior gave the apostles a commandment as to friends and faithful ones, as he had likewise given one to Adam our father before he sinned. But after the sin it was no longer a commandment of fellowship and kinship, of love and brotherhood. He decreed instead a judgment of fearful severity, namely on those who despise the decrees of the law, as Moses also says: "Cursed is everyone who does not abide by the ordinances of this book."

Therefore the Savior both urged what had been said in the law and approved what had been given before the law to those most blessed men. In this way he joined his own teaching to theirs. He thus united the many believers from among the circumcised and also brought in those who lived by nature, that is, the Gentiles who believed. And he condemned the unbelief of the Jews who refused, and of others, and the ignorance shared by both.
